text: WHY ATTEND THE Optica Industry Summit on Aerospace & Defense, 9 to 10 December 2026  A spool of ordinary optical fibre, unwinding behind a first person view drone. The fibre carries the control signals and the video. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Fibre tethered drones are now standard equipment on both sides in Ukraine, and NATO militaries are studying them closely.  Nobody's photonics roadmap predicted that. It came from an operational problem, solved with one of the cheapest optical components our industry makes. Photonics did not enter this fight because it was elegant. It entered because the electromagnetic spectrum became contested.  That is one direction of travel. Here is the other.  TTM Technologies has just reported its first billion-dollar quarter, with aerospace and defence at 37 percent of net sales and program backlog above $1.7 billion. In the same release it announced agreements to acquire Swiss Technology Corporation Group and ILFA GmbH in Germany, its entry into Europe.  Read those two facts together and you can see the shape of the next five years. American interconnect capacity is buying its way into Europe, at the same moment European NATO members are under pressure to build domestic defence electronics capacity of their own.  Sovereign capability is not a slogan. It is a question about who owns the factory.  Catherine Gridley runs TTM's aerospace and defence business and opened the company's new Ultra-HDI plant in Syracuse in June. She is a featured speaker at our summit in December, and she is the right person to ask what it actually takes to get a photonic component into a defence programme.  The programme is built in two halves. Day one is what is being deployed now: directed energy, ISR and optical payloads, autonomous navigation and positioning. Day two is whether the industry can supply it: secure optical and quantum communications, sovereign capability, dual-use transition, multi-domain architectures.  Alongside Cathie are Robert Afzal of Lockheed Martin and Gregory Quarles of Applied Energetics, Inc. on directed energy, Ben Allison of IPG Photonics, Bruno Desruelle and Benjamin Johnson of Exail, Andrew Shields of 東芝 Europe on quantum communications, and Michael Hochberg on how technology crosses from commercial into defence.  Exail hosts us at IXCAMPUS, which is its own kind of signal. Exail has agreed to be acquired by 泰雷茲 at a 3.9 billion euro enterprise value. European defence photonics is consolidating into national champions while American capacity buys in from outside.  We are reviewing registrations to keep the room weighted toward people making build and buy decisions rather than people selling into them.  9 to 10 December 2026, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, just outside Paris.  Which photonics ends up inside European defence programmes will be settled in the next few years, largely by people who already know each other. That is the real argument for being in the room In December. Registration now open.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Yunnan Chihong Zinc&Germanium Co., Ltd. scaling 6 inch substrates, San'An Optoelectronics Co., Ltd. running substrate to chip in a single house. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. THE DEMCON 2026 PHOTONICS GRAND TOUR & THE BIG OPPORTUNITIES Demcon is one of Optica's largest engineering corporate members, and it has recently set up a dedicated photonics division. I spent a day there with the managing director for Demcon photonics, Thijs Kniknie, and it was quite an experience.  We discussed a lot in this interview. From their existing collaborations in space and in-house manufacturing to the catalytic role they are playing in several regions of the world, including  #Enschede.  One highlight for me was a system built under an EU Horizon project for analysing microfluidic samples, designed to detect pathogens in blood and other fluids. Look inside the box and you see how much has to work together. The sample sits on a microfluidic chip that carries a passive photonic element. An active element at the back of the machine aligns to that chip with six degrees of freedom, reads it out using Raman spectroscopy, and processes the data on board before the operator swaps in the next chip. Photonics, mechatronics, microfluidics and medical compliance, all in one enclosure, with DEMCON having developed the complete electronics and mechanics.   Then Thijs Kniknie raised something bigger. DEMCON is working on laser writing technologies that can write waveguides in situ and remove the need for active alignment. Everyone in this field understands that active alignment will not carry us to the volumes photonics needs. Solving that is a scaling problem, not a lab problem. So here is the open call. DEMCON wants to talk to two kinds of companies: those with a laser writing process proven at lab scale that needs to become real equipment, and those with the technology and a product to sell who need the machine to make it.  If that is you, contact Thijs directly, mentioning this Optica video interview. Who will step forward?

WHEN THE DRONE TETHER IS MADE OF GLASS  I listened to a 英國廣播公司 Radio 4 documentary this week called Britain's Robot Army. One passing detail stopped me, and I think it belongs to our industry rather than to the defence press.  The drones reshaping the front line in Ukraine are increasingly guided by a bare optical fibre paying out from a spool bolted to the airframe. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Nobody said who makes that fibre. So we went and found out.  Three things worth your attention.  It is not a bespoke defence product. It is ITU-T G.657.A2 bend-insensitive single-mode fibre, the same category developed for tight-radius routing in fibre-to-the-home. 1310 and 1550 nm, 250 micron coating, dynamic bend radius down to about 7.5 mm. The property that lets you turn a corner in an apartment block is the property that lets a drone unspool 30 km at speed without macrobend loss.  Fibre-guided drones and AI data centres are now bidding for the same product. Chinese cable went from 16 yuan per kilometre in January 2025 to 40 yuan in January 2026, according to Vedomosti via the Kyiv Post. Russia and Ukraine together consume an estimated 50 to 60 million fibre-kilometres a year. The upstream constraint appears to be preform capacity, which nobody expands quickly. A commodity telecom fibre has acquired a second, price-inelastic customer base, and our industry did not plan for that.  The specialist value has moved from the glass to the spool. Nobody draws fibre for drones. What matters is winding geometry, packing process, tension control and payout mechanics, because failures in flight are mechanical rather than optical. The firms doing that work well are small, European and American, and most of them are not yet part of our community. If you would find that session useful, or you work on any part of this chain, from preform to spool to detection, say so in the comments, and we will shape the agenda accordingly. EXPLORING PUBLIC CPO FOUNDRY ROADMAPS  Only four foundries have put a real co-packaged optics roadmap in public: TSMC, Intel, Samsung and GlobalFoundries. Tom's Hardware has broken all four down, and it is worth your weekend or holiday catch-up having a look.  The useful part is that these are not four versions of one plan. They are four business models, and that decides where the rest of us can sell.  台積電 is building a closed platform tied to its own packaging, moving the optical engine from the board, to the substrate beside a switch ASIC, to the interposer inside the package at 12.8 Tbps.   英特爾 is narrower on purpose: an optical chiplet that attaches to compute over PCIe, aimed at CPUs and accelerators, explicitly not at switches.   三星電子 has the longest ladder on paper, ending with lasers integrated alongside compute and memory from 2030.   GlobalFoundries is the outlier and the one that leaves room for everyone else, selling bespoke, standards-compliant optical engines that customers package themselves.  Two things I would take from all this.  Energy is becoming the unit of account. Samsung's public numbers run from roughly 10 picojoules per bit today, to 5, to 2 at interposer integration. Component roadmaps should be written against that scale.  The laser stays outside the package longest. On the most aggressive roadmap published, full integration does not arrive until 2030. Until then lasers, fibre array units, alignment and test remain open, and that is precisely where European suppliers are strong.  Full piece below. Credit to Anton Shilov for the reporting. Today, the German Government laid the foundation for the world's first commercial laser fusion power plant, built in Germany.   The German Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt has announced funding for the Laser Fusion Hub — anchored by a new Fusion R&D campus around European XFEL in Hamburg/Schleswig-Holstein, with a second fusion industrialization site in Biblis, Hesse.   Marvel Fusion and Focused Energy are co-founders of the hub, building it together with partners around the Fusion R&D campus, including EuropeanXFEL, DESY, the University of Hamburg, Christian Albrecht University of Kiel, the University of Rostock, and a growing ecosystem of industrial and scientific partners.   This is bigger than one company or one lab. It's an industry-led hub, open to the full ecosystem, drawing on decades of laser expertise from DESY and the unmatched diagnostic capabilities of European XFEL. The first five research projects — spanning ignition physics, target design, optics durability, laser & plasma diagnostics, and target metrology — have been invited to the second stage of the proposal process, each targeting a concrete milestone on the path to a fusion power plant.   Fusion energy — unlimited, safe, baseload power — is no longer a distant ambition. PROMISED UPDATE: Japanese chip plants restart after Kumamoto earthquake Semiconductor facilities in the Kumamoto area began restarting within days of Tuesday's magnitude 7.1 earthquake. Renesas Electronics resumed production at its Nishiki plant on Wednesday night after confirming clean room integrity and expects its Kawashiri plant in Kumamoto city, in operation since 1970, to restart on 5 August despite wall cracks and water leaks. Tokyo Electron resumed partial operations at Koshi and Ozu from Thursday with full-scale production possible from Monday, and president Toshiki Kawai said the earnings impact should be minor. Mitsubishi Electric restarted some power chip production at Kikuchi and Koshi on Thursday afternoon. 台積電 and 索尼 had not set timelines for their Kikuyo plants as of Thursday evening, with TSMC citing equipment adjustment work. Toshiya Suzuki of Omdia [OPTICA CORPORATE MEMBER] attributed the speed of recovery to seismic isolation in fab construction and to business continuity planning.  What this means: The recovery time is the real story. A decade ago, the same region took roughly three months to restore chip production; this time, most plants are back up and running within a week, and Sony expects pre-quake output by mid-August. Geographic concentration risk in Kumamoto has not gone away, but the cost of that risk has fallen sharply, which weakens one argument European policymakers have used for onshoring. Suppliers of contamination-sensitive optical and metrology equipment should note the specific failure mode reported by TSMC suppliers: impurity accumulation in process equipment that requires cleaning or replacement, rather than structural damage.  One more thing: Japan has joined Horizon Europe.

AT LAST! - PHOTONICS MOVES UP IN THE UNITED KINGDOM. The UK just quietly redefined what counts as a semiconductor company. Photonics is now inside the line.  The UK Dept for Science, Industry and Tech (DSIT) has published the 2026 UK Semiconductor Sectoral Analysis. Mainstream media will headline these numbers: 703 companies, £10.6bn in revenue, £7.5bn GVA, 16,350 direct jobs. But while researching for the panels at 2026 Optica's GPEF in Malaga, I discovered this interesting detail in endnote ix.  "Companies designing, developing or manufacturing photonic integrated circuits (PICs) were classified as dedicated." In the 2024 baseline, a PIC company sat in the diversified bucket. A company that touches semiconductors.   In 2026 it is a semiconductor company BY DEFINITION. That matters, because the dedicated cohort is what DSIT measures, funds and calibrates policy against.  The rest of the report is consistent with that shift:  Photonic IC design and fabrication took 11% of new UK semiconductor research funding in 2024 and 2025. 4th largest category.  Integrated photonics is named as a UK strength, with three geographies attached: Southampton, Glasgow, Northern Ireland.  The top UK assignee of granted US semiconductor patents in 2024 and 2025 is ROCKLEY PHOTONICS LIMITED. That's above Arm.  And the argument the report makes for why: photonic interconnect is part of the AI compute stack "where the UK can compete on capability rather than capital intensity." That is an honest statement about what a country without leading-edge fab capital can realistically hold.  Now the part that should worry people.  The report's own photonics recommendation is a dedicated photonics pilot line and scale-up facility, to bridge UK research to production. It sits in the horizon scanning chapter. No budget. No timeline. No named owner.  Meanwhile, on 30 July, the European Commission opened bidding on up to seven AI Gigafactories, more than €30bn, closing 12 November, awards early 2027, construction from 2027.  To be clear: the UK report never mentions the EU initiative, and the EU initiative never mentions photonics. There is no documented link, and I am not claiming one.  But the industrial logic is hard to miss. The UK has identified photonic ICs for data communications as its near-term opportunity in the second wave of AI-driven demand. Europe has just committed to building the facilities that generate that demand. UK entities cannot join an AI Gigafactory consortium, since the UK is not a EuroHPC Participating State. They can supply into one.  Supplying requires manufacturing capability that exists before the procurement, not after it.  The UK has correctly identified where it can win. The infrastructure to act on it is still a bullet point.  Full read-through in the attached Pozo Strategic Analysis.  SOURCES: https://lnkd.in/eMkgQvhf  EU call: https://lnkd.in/eTvrCG_J

CALLING Optica CORPORATE MEMBERS: THE NEXT-GENERATION RGB LIGHT ENGINE is ready for testing. Details below. I spent a day in  #Enschede, The Netherlands with Tim Tiek, CEO of Brilliance RGB, witnessing a small team turn silicon nitride photonic integrated circuits into a full RGB light engine, small enough for AR glasses and thin enough for a car dashboard. PICs have lived mainly in datacom and telecom for two decades. Brilliance RGB, founded about three years ago, is pushing the same platform into a market with far higher volume: visible light for AR/VR eyewear, automotive displays, and industrial sensing. The chip integrates lasers, waveguides, and sensors onto a single wafer-scale silicon nitride platform, replacing the lenses, prisms, and discrete lasers that make traditional RGB projectors (including IMAX) bulky and expensive.  Why silicon nitride specifically? It couples laser light into waveguides with very high efficiency, which matters most for eyewear: a glasses form factor with a battery that has to last a full day of projection lives or dies on power efficiency. Tim's case for laser displays over micro-LED comes down to full colour, wide field of view, and outdoor brightness, though he's clear micro-LED still wins for simple monochrome use cases like sport glasses.  The automotive angle is just as concrete. Today's heads-up displays run on LCOS panels behind the steering wheel, bulky and lossy by design. Brilliance's approach could shrink that by a factor of ten while cutting cooling overhead, and the same chip architecture could support ground projection as self-driving cars start signalling turns and warnings to pedestrians. Tim's team is already in conversations with Tier 1 suppliers and OEMs on that.  Credibility is building fast for a three-year-old company. Google's Bernard Kress, speaking at the recent Optica summit at 康寧公司, has publicly called PICs a promising technology for next-gen AR/VR goggles, and Brilliance RGB is active in the growing laser-display ecosystem, alongside more than 40 companies now working on laser projection as a category. Brilliance has working prototypes, packaged chips, and active design studies with customers. The next test is scale: moving from hundreds of units today to the volumes consumer electronics and automotive demand, using local foundry and packaging partners in Enschede now, with eight-inch foundry partners lined up for high-volume production.  If you're an Optica corporate member and want to test Brilliance's RGB light engine yourself, reach out to Tim Tiek directly by mentioning this LinkedIn post, or contact me at Optica for an introduction.

AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale.  In other news: Axonal Networks has been named a semifinalist in SEMI's Startups for Sustainable Semiconductors (S3) program, in the New Frontiers in Sustainable Computing category. 33 startups were selected for the virtual pitch event coming up this week on July 29-30, with 10-12 finalists advancing to pitch live at SEMICON West 2026 in San Francisco this October. BREAKING: 7.1 MAGNITUDE EARTHQUAKE hits Kumamoto, home to TSMC's Kyushu chip hub: A magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Japan's Kumamoto Prefecture at 4:35 p.m. local time today, registering the maximum level 7 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale. A magnitude 4.5 aftershock followed four minutes later. The Japan Meteorological Agency placed the epicentre near the city of Uki, at a depth of 10 km, and issued a tsunami advisory for the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas. Roughly 45,600 households in the prefecture lost power, according to Kyushu Electric Power. Why this matters beyond Japan: Kumamoto is home to 台積電's JASM plant, the company's flagship Kyushu investment and a centrepiece of Japan's semiconductor revival. A TSMC spokesperson told Kyodo News the company is currently assessing the situation. No damage or production impact has been confirmed as of this writing.  Worth remembering: a sequence of major earthquakes hit Kumamoto in April 2016, killing 278 people and injuring roughly 2,800. Sony's image sensor plant in the prefecture was knocked offline for more than three months afterwards, disrupting camera sensor supply globally. That's not a prediction of what happens this time. It's a reminder of how concentrated this region's manufacturing footprint has become since then, with TSMC's presence added on top.  Following a request from the Governor of Kumamoto, the Self-Defence Forces are currently operating in the disaster-hit areas with 3,600 personnel. "At this critical situation, guided by the principle of ‘human life first’, we are working in close cooperation with local authorities to minimise damage as much as possible and ensure the safety of the public." What to watch next: Apart from human casualties, TSMC's formal damage assessment, any word on JASM's fourth-quarter mass production timeline, and whether other Kyushu-based suppliers report disruptions.  I'll post an update once TSMC issues a formal statement.  Sources: Nikkei Asia, Akane Okutsu, July 28, 2026  Japan Times: Tsunami alert issued after powerful magnitude 7.1 quake strikes Kumamoto US News: Magnitude 7.1 Earthquake Hits Japan's Kyushu Region/

CHINA ADDS POLISH VIGO Photonics TO EXPORT CONTROL LIST in response to EU-Russia sanctions. China's Ministry of Commerce announced on 24 July that it has added 14 EU entities, including Germany's Rheinmetall and Poland-based infrared detector and laser maker VIGO Photonics S.A., to its export control list, banning the export of dual-use items to them with immediate effect. The ministry framed the move as protecting national security and fulfilling non-proliferation obligations. Adam Piotrowski CEO of VIGO Photonics said, in comments carried by Reuters, that being placed on the list would not have a critical impact on its operations.  What this means:  This is a rare case of a named, publicly listed European photonics company being caught up directly in the EU-China sanctions exchange, rather than the larger defence and general semiconductor names that typically populate such lists. Even though Vigo Photonics has played down the operational impact, the listing signals that Beijing is willing to reach into the mid-cap photonics and infrared-sensing supply chain when retaliating against Brussels, a factor European photonics companies with any China-linked supply chain should now weigh in compliance and sourcing planning. That Beijing's response followed the EU's sanctions package by only a day, and matched its scale one-for-one, is widely read by trade analysts as a deliberate signal rather than a coincidence. However, China's own statement does not frame it that way.  Sources: CGTN; Reuters, via TradingView

LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

Photon Bridge BREAKTHROUGH TOUR 2026 : We visited Photon Bridge in  #Eindhoven in early July, ten months after our first chat at the ECOC Exhibition in Copenhagen. What we saw at their business office on the campus of Eindhoven University of Technology was proof of something the industry doubted was possible: passive self-alignment of indium phosphide lasers onto silicon photonic chips, at insertion losses below 0.6 dB.  Here is why that matters. Combining III-V material, which generates light, with silicon photonics, which routes it cheaply at scale, has always meant trading performance for manufacturability. PhotonBridge's fix: a MEMS structure of flexible cantilevers that lets the III-V die find its own position on the silicon wafer. No active alignment, no per-chip tuning. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. Scottish space company Craft Prospect is already working on using satellites to facilitate Quantum Key Distribution from space – a vital step in scaling these networks from regional to global models.  For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align.  This ties in perfectly with the work being done by QURECA, which was recently highlighted at the Quantum ARC event in Glasgow. That marked the launch of a new report titled ‘Inside Scotland’s Quantum Ecosystem’ – yet another reminder of the country’s key role in the quantum race.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

艾司摩爾 KEYNOTE: CALL FOR OPEN COLLABORATION IN PHOTONICS. The session opened with a direct announcement: next year's GAMA meeting will be hosted by 艾司摩爾 at its campus in Veldhoven, The Netherlands 12 – 13 May 2027. Mark that date in the calendar. That distinction matters for anyone in the room building components for the photonics supply chain.  The first half covered Moore's Law and packaging. Niesing argued that the scaling roadmap remains valid through 2042 but now requires a 16x improvement in compute per two-year cycle -- impossible on 2D scaling alone. The answer is heterogeneous 3D integration, and package sizes are growing as fast as devices are shrinking. ASML's response is a new lithography system with a 4x larger exposure field (52 by 68mm), designed specifically for the interposer layer where logic, memory and photonics converge. IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

ELEPHANTS IN THE ROOM? We continue our deep-tech coverage of last week's Optica GAMA meeting in Brussels, with keynotes now on YouTube from PhotonHub https://lnkd.in/eyZubp7u, IBM https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz and Intel Foundry https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN. Ignazio Piacentini (IP Consulting), who works on assembly and test rather than devices, put it plainly. The story from day one was high-volume manufacturing, and it all turns on co-packaged optics and massive optical interconnect. As he put it, ficonTEC is not moving from 1.0 to 2.0. It is heading to 3.0, and the rest of the equipment base will have to follow.  Then Andrea Rocchetto (EPHOS) raised the point that stayed with me. Two weeks ago the The Royal Society in London ran a photonics war game with three blocks. The West played IP as its strength. China played mass-scale volume manufacturing. South East Asia played its card in advanced packaging. The result was a clear win for China. Andrea would like to run the same game with an audience like this one, which is far more technical and informed. So would I. The rules and the final report are published on the Royal Society site so we hope to investigate further.   That is the elephant. We have the IP. We are short on the volume. The encouraging part is who was in the room. Bert Jan Offrein (IBM), Bernard Lee (SENKO), Sébastien Libon (ESA), Alexander Kessel (Intego), Lars Benesch (Photonics Supply and Services Partner) and others. And when it comes to semiconductor manufacturing at scale, Europe does have a world leader, which is why we opened Day 2 with a keynote and an announcement from Henk Niesing, head of technology at ASML. INTEL KEYNOTE: Advanced packaging as the critical enabler. GRAB A COFFEE AND DON'T MISS THIS! Feeds from last week's GAMA meeting in Brussels have started all kinds of conversations. I am sure this will be another one. Watch this presentation on YouTube: https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN  Nick Psaila, formerly of OptoScribe and now leading co-packaged optics (CPO) development at Intel Foundry, delivered an excellent keynote at Optica Gamma Brussels 2026. His talk cut straight to the core problem: AI systems are no longer compute-limited, they are IO-limited, and copper interconnects are running out of road.  Psaila laid out why CPO is not a future technology but a present-tense supply chain emergency. With at least five one-gigawatt data centres expected online this year, and projections of over 100 million 1600G-equivalent optical links per facility, he warned the entire photonics supply chain, from PIC fabs to FAU manufacturers to assembly and metrology equipment providers, that volume investment is required now.  The talk then moved into advanced packaging as the critical enabler. Psaila argued that CPO is as much a packaging challenge as a photonics one, and that the industry needs to abandon artisan assembly processes in favour of wafer-level, high-throughput, JEDEC-qualified manufacturing compatible with heterogeneous integration and 3D stacking. He outlined Intel's packaging spectrum from EMIB to Foveros, and introduced their work on glass core substrates, including the first demonstration of a 24-layer glass core with embedded EMIB presented at ECTC the previous week. Glass core, he argued, solves the CTE mismatch problem that increasingly limits organic substrates at large panel sizes, and opens a path to integrating 3D waveguides directly into the substrate for in-package optical interconnects.  He closed with a long-range vision: panel-scale compute with an embedded optical connectivity matrix that routes signals from die-to-die to the external network within a single architecture.  The Q&A that followed was one of the more direct exchanges of the day. It has been edited out of this version. Representatives from Opsydia, Ephos, and FEMTOPRINT SA each weighed in on their own approaches to direct laser writing for in-package waveguides, with Rolando Ferrini from FEMTOPRINT SA making the pointed argument that the industry cannot rely on a single supplier at this scale and that cross-licensing between European competitors may ultimately serve the market better than winner-takes-all competition. A voice-of-the-customer moment from Peter Kirkegaard cut through the noise: demand will be high enough that there is work for everyone. Further questions addressed polymer microoptics and their reliability constraints under reflow and TCB conditions, as well as how companies like Demcon Photonics are working to bring direct laser writing processes into foundry-compatible, high-volume manufacturing. For me, one of the best presentations in a long time. Agree?

While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. LEARN FROM Lumentum: BORROWED FROM SEMICONDUCTORS, BUILT FOR PHOTONICS: THE PACKAGING MOVE AI CONNECTIVITY NEEDS At Optica GAMA last week (June 2-3 2026), Matt Guzy, Advanced Packaging lead at Lumentum, did something rare: he showed us a working prototype and explained exactly how it was built. Watch his presentation here https://lnkd.in/gR9EyFYu.   Matt came to Lumentum after 21 years at Intel, where he worked on some of the earliest heterogeneous integration in client computing, including glass-core substrates and early chiplet stacking. He brought that background to a deceptively simple question: how do you package VCSELs with CMOS in a way that's actually manufacturable?  His answer was fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) - a process already running at volume in your smartphone. He dropped III-V VCSEL die, photodiodes, a TIA and a driver into a standard OSAT flow, following existing design rules without inventing a single new process step. The result: a compact optic engine 17.5 x 5.6mm - roughly the size of a tic-tac - capable of 12.8 Tb/s across 80 channels at 50 Gbps per channel, at under 2.5 pJ/bit, with bandwidth density above 1.5 Tb/s per millimeter.  The engineering choices were deliberate. He wanted to de-risk everything downstream - fibre integration, board validation, test - so he kept the assembly flow completely conventional. That discipline is what allowed the team to debut the package at OFC earlier this year.  Matt's broader point was equally sharp: the photonics industry doesn't need to repeat the painful early years of advanced semiconductor packaging. The yield learning, the process infrastructure, the OSAT ecosystem - it already exists. The opportunity is to design optical solutions around what works, rather than starting from scratch.  On standards, he was pragmatic: wait 12 to 18 months. The field is too fragmented today to standardise usefully. When two or three approaches pull ahead, standards will follow naturally and will actually mean something.  On the VCSEL vs. external laser question: he was clear-eyed. VCSELs are not a universal answer. They don't have the reach for scale-across applications. But for within-rack and rack-to-rack, they offer a lower-cost, lower-power, high-bandwidth option that doesn't require reinventing the supply chain.  The photonics community tends to treat packaging as a downstream problem. Matt's work suggests it should be the starting point.

WHY CO-PACKAGED OPTICS FAILED IN 2011 - AND WHY IT WON'T THIS TIME. At the Optica GAMA Meeting last week (June 2-3 2026), Bert Jan Offrein of IBM Research Zurich opened with a question that cuts to the heart of where photonics stands today: why, after IBM deployed co-packaged optics in a supercomputer back in 2011, did the industry walk away from it for a decade? The answer matters because we're back at the same junction. Follow the link below to watch the 21-minute presentation on the Optica YouTube channel. https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz.  In 2011, optics lost to a workaround. The ratio of communication to compute dropped from roughly one byte per flop to less than one hundredth. Electrical systems adapted, and the assembly overhead of optics - the lasers, modulators, drivers, alignment tolerances, fiber routing - simply wasn't worth it.  That trade-off no longer works. AI training and inference have reversed the pressure. We're back to multi-chip modules, back to bandwidth walls, and back to optics as the only credible path forward. SABIC GRAND TOUR AND THE CHALLENGE OF REFLOW SOLDERING On our way to Belgium, Optica just visited 沙特基礎工業公司's Opto-Electronic Centre of Excellence in Bergen op Zoom, The Netherlands. We got the full tour with Gabrie Hoogland and Young Joon Choi to understand how new materials can solve one problem that catches optical designers off guard: reflow soldering. The interview is 30 minutes and is therefore available on YouTube.   JEDEC protocols run at 260°C, three passes. Most thermoplastic resins deform at that temperature. Most optical designers discover this at the packaging stage, not the design stage.  沙特基礎工業公司 developed Extem - a thermoplastic polyimide with a glass transition temperature of 280°C - specifically to close that gap. It survives reflow, can be injection moulded with 5nm surface roughness and sub-micron dimensional tolerances, and is capable of millions of parts per year. Three things stood out from the visit:  1. Alignment before reflow is now possible. Package your optics on the board first, then solder. That changes the economics for OSAT companies.  2. Epoxy is avoidable. Extem and Ultem can be metallised and self-aligned on a PCB via solder paste capillary action. No adhesive required.  3. Detachable connectors work. A demonstrator built with Tyndall National Institute showed 2.2 dB penalty over 40 make-and-break cycles using expanded beam microlens arrays. The loss came from the PIC design, not the lenses. So, if you are designing for co-packaged optics and have not checked your material's reflow compatibility, check now.  Interested in more information? WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Yunnan Chihong Zinc&Germanium Co., Ltd. scaling 6 inch substrates, San'An Optoelectronics Co., Ltd. running substrate to chip in a single house. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. WHEN THE DRONE TETHER IS MADE OF GLASS  I listened to a 英國廣播公司 Radio 4 documentary this week called Britain's Robot Army. One passing detail stopped me, and I think it belongs to our industry rather than to the defence press.  The drones reshaping the front line in Ukraine are increasingly guided by a bare optical fibre paying out from a spool bolted to the airframe. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Nobody said who makes that fibre. So we went and found out.  Three things worth your attention.  It is not a bespoke defence product. It is ITU-T G.657.A2 bend-insensitive single-mode fibre, the same category developed for tight-radius routing in fibre-to-the-home. 1310 and 1550 nm, 250 micron coating, dynamic bend radius down to about 7.5 mm. The property that lets you turn a corner in an apartment block is the property that lets a drone unspool 30 km at speed without macrobend loss.  Fibre-guided drones and AI data centres are now bidding for the same product. Chinese cable went from 16 yuan per kilometre in January 2025 to 40 yuan in January 2026, according to Vedomosti via the Kyiv Post. Russia and Ukraine together consume an estimated 50 to 60 million fibre-kilometres a year. The upstream constraint appears to be preform capacity, which nobody expands quickly. A commodity telecom fibre has acquired a second, price-inelastic customer base, and our industry did not plan for that.  The specialist value has moved from the glass to the spool. Nobody draws fibre for drones. What matters is winding geometry, packing process, tension control and payout mechanics, because failures in flight are mechanical rather than optical. The firms doing that work well are small, European and American, and most of them are not yet part of our community. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

META IS SELLING THE THING IT SAID IT NEEDED MORE OF Meta just admitted it has more AI compute than it knows what to do with. That single fact explains more about the state of the AI trade than any earnings call this quarter. On July 1, Bloomberg reported Meta is building a new unit, internally called Meta Compute, to sell its spare GPU capacity to outside customers. Two models are reportedly on the table: hosted access to Meta's own AI (including its new Muse Spark model, the AWS Bedrock playbook) or straight compute rental, the CoreWeave playbook. The unit is said to be run by infrastructure chief Santosh Janardhan, Superintelligence Labs lead Daniel Gross, and president Dina Powell McCormick.  The market's reaction tells you where the real anxiety sits. Meta stock jumped more than 10% that day, its best single session in five months, after a year in which the stock had fallen close to 15% and lagged the S&P 500. CoreWeave fell 10.8%. Nebius fell 12.4%. Meta has committed roughly $48 billion to renting GPUs from those two companies (a $21 billion CoreWeave deal, expanded in April, plus up to $27 billion with Nebius) because its own buildout couldn't keep pace with demand. If Meta suddenly has capacity to spare, either its infrastructure finally caught up, or the demand it built for never fully showed up.  That's the case Ed Zitron made to Ed Elson on this week's Prof G Markets. Meta still doesn't break out Meta AI or Llama revenue the way Google or OpenAI report their AI businesses, so reselling the leftover GPUs is the clearest return Meta can point to on its spending so far. Zitron's broader argument, laid out in his newsletter, is that most of the AI capex boom is really being justified by two customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, who account for the bulk of the industry's disclosed AI revenue. Strip them out and the rest of the "AI economy" thins out fast. As he posted on X the day the story broke: "We'll know we will hit the top when Meta sells compute to Anthropic."  Worth a counterpoint. WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.
