WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.
Excellent summary. Worth your time reading.

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

ELEPHANTS IN THE ROOM? We continue our deep-tech coverage of last week's Optica GAMA meeting in Brussels, with keynotes now on YouTube from PhotonHub https://lnkd.in/eyZubp7u, IBM https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz and Intel Foundry https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN. Andrea would like to run the same game with an audience like this one, which is far more technical and informed. So would I. Bert Jan Offrein (IBM), Bernard Lee (SENKO), Sébastien Libon (ESA), Alexander Kessel (Intego), Lars Benesch (Photonics Supply and Services Partner) and others. And when it comes to semiconductor manufacturing at scale, Europe does have a world leader, which is why we opened Day 2 with a keynote and an announcement from Henk Niesing, head of technology at ASML. INTEL KEYNOTE: Advanced packaging as the critical enabler. GRAB A COFFEE AND DON'T MISS THIS! Feeds from last week's GAMA meeting in Brussels have started all kinds of conversations. I am sure this will be another one. Watch this presentation on YouTube: https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN  Nick Psaila, formerly of OptoScribe and now leading co-packaged optics (CPO) development at Intel Foundry, delivered an excellent keynote at Optica Gamma Brussels 2026. His talk cut straight to the core problem: AI systems are no longer compute-limited, they are IO-limited, and copper interconnects are running out of road. The talk then moved into advanced packaging as the critical enabler. Psaila argued that CPO is as much a packaging challenge as a photonics one, and that the industry needs to abandon artisan assembly processes in favour of wafer-level, high-throughput, JEDEC-qualified manufacturing compatible with heterogeneous integration and 3D stacking. He outlined Intel's packaging spectrum from EMIB to Foveros, and introduced their work on glass core substrates, including the first demonstration of a 24-layer glass core with embedded EMIB presented at ECTC the previous week. Glass core, he argued, solves the CTE mismatch problem that increasingly limits organic substrates at large panel sizes, and opens a path to integrating 3D waveguides directly into the substrate for in-package optical interconnects.  He closed with a long-range vision: panel-scale compute with an embedded optical connectivity matrix that routes signals from die-to-die to the external network within a single architecture.  The Q&A that followed was one of the more direct exchanges of the day. It has been edited out of this version. Further questions addressed polymer microoptics and their reliability constraints under reflow and TCB conditions, as well as how companies like Demcon Photonics are working to bring direct laser writing processes into foundry-compatible, high-volume manufacturing. For me, one of the best presentations in a long time. Agree?

While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. LEARN FROM Lumentum: BORROWED FROM SEMICONDUCTORS, BUILT FOR PHOTONICS: THE PACKAGING MOVE AI CONNECTIVITY NEEDS At Optica GAMA last week (June 2-3 2026), Matt Guzy, Advanced Packaging lead at Lumentum, did something rare: he showed us a working prototype and explained exactly how it was built. Watch his presentation here https://lnkd.in/gR9EyFYu.   Matt came to Lumentum after 21 years at Intel, where he worked on some of the earliest heterogeneous integration in client computing, including glass-core substrates and early chiplet stacking. He brought that background to a deceptively simple question: how do you package VCSELs with CMOS in a way that's actually manufacturable?  His answer was fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) - a process already running at volume in your smartphone. He dropped III-V VCSEL die, photodiodes, a TIA and a driver into a standard OSAT flow, following existing design rules without inventing a single new process step. The result: a compact optic engine 17.5 x 5.6mm - roughly the size of a tic-tac - capable of 12.8 Tb/s across 80 channels at 50 Gbps per channel, at under 2.5 pJ/bit, with bandwidth density above 1.5 Tb/s per millimeter.  The engineering choices were deliberate. He wanted to de-risk everything downstream - fibre integration, board validation, test - so he kept the assembly flow completely conventional. That discipline is what allowed the team to debut the package at OFC earlier this year.  Matt's broader point was equally sharp: the photonics industry doesn't need to repeat the painful early years of advanced semiconductor packaging. The yield learning, the process infrastructure, the OSAT ecosystem - it already exists. The opportunity is to design optical solutions around what works, rather than starting from scratch.  On standards, he was pragmatic: wait 12 to 18 months. The field is too fragmented today to standardise usefully. When two or three approaches pull ahead, standards will follow naturally and will actually mean something.  On the VCSEL vs. external laser question: he was clear-eyed. VCSELs are not a universal answer. They don't have the reach for scale-across applications. But for within-rack and rack-to-rack, they offer a lower-cost, lower-power, high-bandwidth option that doesn't require reinventing the supply chain.  The photonics community tends to treat packaging as a downstream problem. Matt's work suggests it should be the starting point.

WHY CO-PACKAGED OPTICS FAILED IN 2011 - AND WHY IT WON'T THIS TIME. At the Optica GAMA Meeting last week (June 2-3 2026), Bert Jan Offrein of IBM Research Zurich opened with a question that cuts to the heart of where photonics stands today: why, after IBM deployed co-packaged optics in a supercomputer back in 2011, did the industry walk away from it for a decade? The answer matters because we're back at the same junction. Follow the link below to watch the 21-minute presentation on the Optica YouTube channel. https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz.  In 2011, optics lost to a workaround. The ratio of communication to compute dropped from roughly one byte per flop to less than one hundredth. Electrical systems adapted, and the assembly overhead of optics - the lasers, modulators, drivers, alignment tolerances, fiber routing - simply wasn't worth it.  That trade-off no longer works. AI training and inference have reversed the pressure. We're back to multi-chip modules, back to bandwidth walls, and back to optics as the only credible path forward. But the overhead problem hasn't gone away.  Bert's argument is that solving it requires rethinking assembly, not just components. IBM's polymer waveguide approach - where light transitions adiabatically from a silicon or silicon nitride chip waveguide into a polymer matched to fiber mode size - enables 100 optical connections in a single flip-chip attach. That's the direction: optical connectivity that integrates into standard electrical assembly flows, is solder-reflow compatible, and is Telcordia-tested.  Further out, a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)-funded project is targeting 3D optical routing with 3-micron waveguide pitch, vertical vias, and chip-to-chip optical bonding through substrates - essentially replicating in the optical domain what the back-end-of-line does electrically.   Current mirror losses are around 1 dB and improving. The practical implication: the technology choices that will define the next generation of AI infrastructure won't be decided by peak performance specs. They'll be decided by who solves the assembly overhead at system level - not just the first-level package, but across the full board and chassis.  IBM Research is now operating as a collaborator rather than a licensor - open to partnerships that can bring these approaches to production. That shift in posture, from IP generator to system integrator, may matter as much as the technology itself.  Bert Jan Offrein presented at the Optica GAMA Meeting, June 2, 2026. Optica brings together the photonics community to accelerate exactly these kinds of industry-critical conversations. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A 50-POUND INSTRUMENT FITS ON A CHIP At the GAMA meeting in Brussels on June 3rd, Diana Mojahed, PhD, CEO of Optica Corporate member Lightfinder (based in Boston USA), closed the conference with something the room had not seen before. Lightfinder has built a chip-based optical spectrum analyzer on standard silicon photonics. No exotic materials. No moving parts. A device that fits in a small enclosure -- and delivers spectral resolution and bandwidth comparable to a Yokogawa OSA that weighs 50 pounds and costs tens of thousands of dollars per unit. The technology is a digital Fourier transform spectrometer: a cascade of Mach-Zehnder interferometers on a silicon photonic chip, using a single photodetector and a Fourier-domain encoding scheme to achieve very competitive resolution. Add one stage to the architecture, and you double your channel count -- an exponential scaling property that conventional dispersive spectrometers simply cannot match.  Why does this matter for our industry? Because co-packaged optics is heading toward volume production, and optical testing has not kept up. ATE companies can run 10,000 electronic tests simultaneously. The optical test is still stuck at one bench instrument per measurement point. LightFinder is building the chip that changes that ratio.  The Optica GAMA audience saw the potential immediately. By the end of the Q&A, there were several offers of a packaging and automation partnership from the floor. Beyond CPO, the platform roadmap covers extended NIR and visible wavelengths—spectroscopy-on-a-chip for semiconductor process control, medical diagnostics, remote sensing, and industrial inspection. The same silicon photonic infrastructure being built for datacenters could produce sensing chips at a volume that rivals CPO itself. If you are working in photonic packaging, test, or sensing -- and you are not already talking to LightFinder -- now is the time. Diana Mojahed can be reached at diana@lightfindertech.com. SABIC GRAND TOUR AND THE CHALLENGE OF REFLOW SOLDERING On our way to Belgium, Optica just visited 沙特基礎工業公司's Opto-Electronic Centre of Excellence in Bergen op Zoom, The Netherlands. We got the full tour with Gabrie Hoogland and Young Joon Choi to understand how new materials can solve one problem that catches optical designers off guard: reflow soldering. The interview is 30 minutes and is therefore available on YouTube.   JEDEC protocols run at 260°C, three passes. Most thermoplastic resins deform at that temperature. Most optical designers discover this at the packaging stage, not the design stage.  沙特基礎工業公司 developed Extem - a thermoplastic polyimide with a glass transition temperature of 280°C - specifically to close that gap. It survives reflow, can be injection moulded with 5nm surface roughness and sub-micron dimensional tolerances, and is capable of millions of parts per year. Three things stood out from the visit:  1. Alignment before reflow is now possible. Package your optics on the board first, then solder. That changes the economics for OSAT companies.  2. Epoxy is avoidable. Extem and Ultem can be metallised and self-aligned on a PCB via solder paste capillary action. No adhesive required.  3. Detachable connectors work. A demonstrator built with Tyndall National Institute showed 2.2 dB penalty over 40 make-and-break cycles using expanded beam microlens arrays. The loss came from the PIC design, not the lenses. So, if you are designing for co-packaged optics and have not checked your material's reflow compatibility, check now.  Interested in more information? AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

WHY ATTEND THE Optica Industry Summit on Aerospace & Defense, 9 to 10 December 2026  A spool of ordinary optical fibre, unwinding behind a first person view drone. The fibre carries the control signals and the video. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Fibre tethered drones are now standard equipment on both sides in Ukraine, and NATO militaries are studying them closely.  Nobody's photonics roadmap predicted that. It came from an operational problem, solved with one of the cheapest optical components our industry makes. Photonics did not enter this fight because it was elegant. It entered because the electromagnetic spectrum became contested.  That is one direction of travel. Here is the other.  TTM Technologies has just reported its first billion-dollar quarter, with aerospace and defence at 37 percent of net sales and program backlog above $1.7 billion. In the same release it announced agreements to acquire Swiss Technology Corporation Group and ILFA GmbH in Germany, its entry into Europe.  Read those two facts together and you can see the shape of the next five years. American interconnect capacity is buying its way into Europe, at the same moment European NATO members are under pressure to build domestic defence electronics capacity of their own.  Sovereign capability is not a slogan. It is a question about who owns the factory. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

Greater Glasgow was recently ranked the fifth most important quantum cluster in the world, and first globally for its role as a sector hub. That’s an incredible achievement for the UK, and a massive nod to Scotland's deep-tech ecosystem.  This week I’ve been following discussions at Optica's Quantum 2.0 Conference in Glasgow (15–18 June) where one of the themes has been the race to translate raw R&D into practical, commercial applications.  Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica, captured the challenge. He pointed out that quantum is currently moving at two separate speeds: academic research (measured in qubits) and industry reality (focused on scalable products). At the moment, they’re not aligned. While the science is forging ahead, the market is lagging in building the next-generation hardware needed to protect our critical infrastructure.  The timeline is tight. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Andrew Shields of Toshiba Europe UK thought a ten-year horizon was more realistic, but there’s great urgency nonetheless. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. Scottish space company Craft Prospect is already working on using satellites to facilitate Quantum Key Distribution from space – a vital step in scaling these networks from regional to global models.  For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align. WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

ELEPHANTS IN THE ROOM? We continue our deep-tech coverage of last week's Optica GAMA meeting in Brussels, with keynotes now on YouTube from PhotonHub https://lnkd.in/eyZubp7u, IBM https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz and Intel Foundry https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN. INTEL KEYNOTE: Advanced packaging as the critical enabler. GRAB A COFFEE AND DON'T MISS THIS! Feeds from last week's GAMA meeting in Brussels have started all kinds of conversations. Watch this presentation on YouTube: https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN  Nick Psaila, formerly of OptoScribe and now leading co-packaged optics (CPO) development at Intel Foundry, delivered an excellent keynote at Optica Gamma Brussels 2026. His talk cut straight to the core problem: AI systems are no longer compute-limited, they are IO-limited, and copper interconnects are running out of road. Glass core, he argued, solves the CTE mismatch problem that increasingly limits organic substrates at large panel sizes, and opens a path to integrating 3D waveguides directly into the substrate for in-package optical interconnects.  He closed with a long-range vision: panel-scale compute with an embedded optical connectivity matrix that routes signals from die-to-die to the external network within a single architecture. While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. LEARN FROM Lumentum: BORROWED FROM SEMICONDUCTORS, BUILT FOR PHOTONICS: THE PACKAGING MOVE AI CONNECTIVITY NEEDS At Optica GAMA last week (June 2-3 2026), Matt Guzy, Advanced Packaging lead at Lumentum, did something rare: he showed us a working prototype and explained exactly how it was built. Watch his presentation here https://lnkd.in/gR9EyFYu.   Matt came to Lumentum after 21 years at Intel, where he worked on some of the earliest heterogeneous integration in client computing, including glass-core substrates and early chiplet stacking. He brought that background to a deceptively simple question: how do you package VCSELs with CMOS in a way that's actually manufacturable?  His answer was fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) - a process already running at volume in your smartphone. He dropped III-V VCSEL die, photodiodes, a TIA and a driver into a standard OSAT flow, following existing design rules without inventing a single new process step. The result: a compact optic engine 17.5 x 5.6mm - roughly the size of a tic-tac - capable of 12.8 Tb/s across 80 channels at 50 Gbps per channel, at under 2.5 pJ/bit, with bandwidth density above 1.5 Tb/s per millimeter.  The engineering choices were deliberate. He wanted to de-risk everything downstream - fibre integration, board validation, test - so he kept the assembly flow completely conventional. That discipline is what allowed the team to debut the package at OFC earlier this year.  Matt's broader point was equally sharp: the photonics industry doesn't need to repeat the painful early years of advanced semiconductor packaging. The yield learning, the process infrastructure, the OSAT ecosystem - it already exists. The opportunity is to design optical solutions around what works, rather than starting from scratch.  On standards, he was pragmatic: wait 12 to 18 months. The field is too fragmented today to standardise usefully. When two or three approaches pull ahead, standards will follow naturally and will actually mean something.  On the VCSEL vs. external laser question: he was clear-eyed. VCSELs are not a universal answer. They don't have the reach for scale-across applications. But for within-rack and rack-to-rack, they offer a lower-cost, lower-power, high-bandwidth option that doesn't require reinventing the supply chain.  The photonics community tends to treat packaging as a downstream problem. Matt's work suggests it should be the starting point.

WHY CO-PACKAGED OPTICS FAILED IN 2011 - AND WHY IT WON'T THIS TIME. At the Optica GAMA Meeting last week (June 2-3 2026), Bert Jan Offrein of IBM Research Zurich opened with a question that cuts to the heart of where photonics stands today: why, after IBM deployed co-packaged optics in a supercomputer back in 2011, did the industry walk away from it for a decade? The answer matters because we're back at the same junction. Follow the link below to watch the 21-minute presentation on the Optica YouTube channel. https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz.  In 2011, optics lost to a workaround. The ratio of communication to compute dropped from roughly one byte per flop to less than one hundredth. Electrical systems adapted, and the assembly overhead of optics - the lasers, modulators, drivers, alignment tolerances, fiber routing - simply wasn't worth it.  That trade-off no longer works. AI training and inference have reversed the pressure. We're back to multi-chip modules, back to bandwidth walls, and back to optics as the only credible path forward. But the overhead problem hasn't gone away.  Bert's argument is that solving it requires rethinking assembly, not just components. IBM's polymer waveguide approach - where light transitions adiabatically from a silicon or silicon nitride chip waveguide into a polymer matched to fiber mode size - enables 100 optical connections in a single flip-chip attach. That's the direction: optical connectivity that integrates into standard electrical assembly flows, is solder-reflow compatible, and is Telcordia-tested.  Further out, a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)-funded project is targeting 3D optical routing with 3-micron waveguide pitch, vertical vias, and chip-to-chip optical bonding through substrates - essentially replicating in the optical domain what the back-end-of-line does electrically.   Current mirror losses are around 1 dB and improving. The practical implication: the technology choices that will define the next generation of AI infrastructure won't be decided by peak performance specs. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale.  In other news: Axonal Networks has been named a semifinalist in SEMI's Startups for Sustainable Semiconductors (S3) program, in the New Frontiers in Sustainable Computing category. 33 startups were selected for the virtual pitch event coming up this week on July 29-30, with 10-12 finalists advancing to pitch live at SEMICON West 2026 in San Francisco this October. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

The message Linque left us with applies to the whole industry: photonics reaching product stage in the data center is not a one-company story. It takes the full semiconductor value chain, from equipment makers and fabs to OSATs, chip designers and system integrators, moving at the speed this buildout demands.

META IS SELLING THE THING IT SAID IT NEEDED MORE OF Meta just admitted it has more AI compute than it knows what to do with. That single fact explains more about the state of the AI trade than any earnings call this quarter. On July 1, Bloomberg reported Meta is building a new unit, internally called Meta Compute, to sell its spare GPU capacity to outside customers. Two models are reportedly on the table: hosted access to Meta's own AI (including its new Muse Spark model, the AWS Bedrock playbook) or straight compute rental, the CoreWeave playbook. The unit is said to be run by infrastructure chief Santosh Janardhan, Superintelligence Labs lead Daniel Gross, and president Dina Powell McCormick.  The market's reaction tells you where the real anxiety sits. Meta stock jumped more than 10% that day, its best single session in five months, after a year in which the stock had fallen close to 15% and lagged the S&P 500. CoreWeave fell 10.8%. Nebius fell 12.4%. Meta has committed roughly $48 billion to renting GPUs from those two companies (a $21 billion CoreWeave deal, expanded in April, plus up to $27 billion with Nebius) because its own buildout couldn't keep pace with demand. If Meta suddenly has capacity to spare, either its infrastructure finally caught up, or the demand it built for never fully showed up.  That's the case Ed Zitron made to Ed Elson on this week's Prof G Markets. Meta still doesn't break out Meta AI or Llama revenue the way Google or OpenAI report their AI businesses, so reselling the leftover GPUs is the clearest return Meta can point to on its spending so far. Zitron's broader argument, laid out in his newsletter, is that most of the AI capex boom is really being justified by two customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, who account for the bulk of the industry's disclosed AI revenue. Strip them out and the rest of the "AI economy" thins out fast. As he posted on X the day the story broke: "We'll know we will hit the top when Meta sells compute to Anthropic."  Worth a counterpoint. SpaceX did something similar with xAI's Colossus 1 site, leasing capacity to Anthropic for roughly $1.25 billion a month and to Google for about $920 million a month, a pair of deals Bloomberg Intelligence estimates could be worth over $50 billion by 2028. Reselling spare capacity isn't automatically a distress signal. It can just as easily be a company admitting it over-built for a demand curve that hasn't arrived on schedule, and doing something rational with the surplus while it waits.  Which gets to the actual question worth asking: who is monetizing AI right now, in dollars, not narrative? Greater Glasgow was recently ranked the fifth most important quantum cluster in the world, and first globally for its role as a sector hub. That’s an incredible achievement for the UK, and a massive nod to Scotland's deep-tech ecosystem.  This week I’ve been following discussions at Optica's Quantum 2.0 Conference in Glasgow (15–18 June) where one of the themes has been the race to translate raw R&D into practical, commercial applications.  Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica, captured the challenge. He pointed out that quantum is currently moving at two separate speeds: academic research (measured in qubits) and industry reality (focused on scalable products). At the moment, they’re not aligned. While the science is forging ahead, the market is lagging in building the next-generation hardware needed to protect our critical infrastructure.  The timeline is tight. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Andrew Shields of Toshiba Europe UK thought a ten-year horizon was more realistic, but there’s great urgency nonetheless. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. Scottish space company Craft Prospect is already working on using satellites to facilitate Quantum Key Distribution from space – a vital step in scaling these networks from regional to global models.  For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align.  This ties in perfectly with the work being done by QURECA, which was recently highlighted at the Quantum ARC event in Glasgow. That marked the launch of a new report titled ‘Inside Scotland’s Quantum Ecosystem’ – yet another reminder of the country’s key role in the quantum race.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

Niesing argued that the scaling roadmap remains valid through 2042 but now requires a 16x improvement in compute per two-year cycle -- impossible on 2D scaling alone. IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

INTEL KEYNOTE: Advanced packaging as the critical enabler. GRAB A COFFEE AND DON'T MISS THIS! Feeds from last week's GAMA meeting in Brussels have started all kinds of conversations. Watch this presentation on YouTube: https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN  Nick Psaila, formerly of OptoScribe and now leading co-packaged optics (CPO) development at Intel Foundry, delivered an excellent keynote at Optica Gamma Brussels 2026. His talk cut straight to the core problem: AI systems are no longer compute-limited, they are IO-limited, and copper interconnects are running out of road.  Psaila laid out why CPO is not a future technology but a present-tense supply chain emergency. With at least five one-gigawatt data centres expected online this year, and projections of over 100 million 1600G-equivalent optical links per facility, he warned the entire photonics supply chain, from PIC fabs to FAU manufacturers to assembly and metrology equipment providers, that volume investment is required now.  The talk then moved into advanced packaging as the critical enabler. Psaila argued that CPO is as much a packaging challenge as a photonics one, and that the industry needs to abandon artisan assembly processes in favour of wafer-level, high-throughput, JEDEC-qualified manufacturing compatible with heterogeneous integration and 3D stacking. He outlined Intel's packaging spectrum from EMIB to Foveros, and introduced their work on glass core substrates, including the first demonstration of a 24-layer glass core with embedded EMIB presented at ECTC the previous week. Glass core, he argued, solves the CTE mismatch problem that increasingly limits organic substrates at large panel sizes, and opens a path to integrating 3D waveguides directly into the substrate for in-package optical interconnects.  He closed with a long-range vision: panel-scale compute with an embedded optical connectivity matrix that routes signals from die-to-die to the external network within a single architecture.  The Q&A that followed was one of the more direct exchanges of the day. It has been edited out of this version. Representatives from Opsydia, Ephos, and FEMTOPRINT SA each weighed in on their own approaches to direct laser writing for in-package waveguides, with Rolando Ferrini from FEMTOPRINT SA making the pointed argument that the industry cannot rely on a single supplier at this scale and that cross-licensing between European competitors may ultimately serve the market better than winner-takes-all competition. A voice-of-the-customer moment from Peter Kirkegaard cut through the noise: demand will be high enough that there is work for everyone. Further questions addressed polymer microoptics and their reliability constraints under reflow and TCB conditions, as well as how companies like Demcon Photonics are working to bring direct laser writing processes into foundry-compatible, high-volume manufacturing. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. LEARN FROM Lumentum: BORROWED FROM SEMICONDUCTORS, BUILT FOR PHOTONICS: THE PACKAGING MOVE AI CONNECTIVITY NEEDS At Optica GAMA last week (June 2-3 2026), Matt Guzy, Advanced Packaging lead at Lumentum, did something rare: he showed us a working prototype and explained exactly how it was built. Watch his presentation here https://lnkd.in/gR9EyFYu.   Matt came to Lumentum after 21 years at Intel, where he worked on some of the earliest heterogeneous integration in client computing, including glass-core substrates and early chiplet stacking. He brought that background to a deceptively simple question: how do you package VCSELs with CMOS in a way that's actually manufacturable?  His answer was fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) - a process already running at volume in your smartphone. He dropped III-V VCSEL die, photodiodes, a TIA and a driver into a standard OSAT flow, following existing design rules without inventing a single new process step. The result: a compact optic engine 17.5 x 5.6mm - roughly the size of a tic-tac - capable of 12.8 Tb/s across 80 channels at 50 Gbps per channel, at under 2.5 pJ/bit, with bandwidth density above 1.5 Tb/s per millimeter.  The engineering choices were deliberate. He wanted to de-risk everything downstream - fibre integration, board validation, test - so he kept the assembly flow completely conventional. That discipline is what allowed the team to debut the package at OFC earlier this year.  Matt's broader point was equally sharp: the photonics industry doesn't need to repeat the painful early years of advanced semiconductor packaging. The yield learning, the process infrastructure, the OSAT ecosystem - it already exists. The opportunity is to design optical solutions around what works, rather than starting from scratch.  On standards, he was pragmatic: wait 12 to 18 months. The field is too fragmented today to standardise usefully. When two or three approaches pull ahead, standards will follow naturally and will actually mean something.  On the VCSEL vs. external laser question: he was clear-eyed. VCSELs are not a universal answer. They don't have the reach for scale-across applications. But for within-rack and rack-to-rack, they offer a lower-cost, lower-power, high-bandwidth option that doesn't require reinventing the supply chain.  The photonics community tends to treat packaging as a downstream problem. Matt's work suggests it should be the starting point.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A 50-POUND INSTRUMENT FITS ON A CHIP At the GAMA meeting in Brussels on June 3rd, Diana Mojahed, PhD, CEO of Optica Corporate member Lightfinder (based in Boston USA), closed the conference with something the room had not seen before. Lightfinder has built a chip-based optical spectrum analyzer on standard silicon photonics. No exotic materials. No moving parts. A device that fits in a small enclosure -- and delivers spectral resolution and bandwidth comparable to a Yokogawa OSA that weighs 50 pounds and costs tens of thousands of dollars per unit. The technology is a digital Fourier transform spectrometer: a cascade of Mach-Zehnder interferometers on a silicon photonic chip, using a single photodetector and a Fourier-domain encoding scheme to achieve very competitive resolution. Add one stage to the architecture, and you double your channel count -- an exponential scaling property that conventional dispersive spectrometers simply cannot match.  Why does this matter for our industry? Because co-packaged optics is heading toward volume production, and optical testing has not kept up. ATE companies can run 10,000 electronic tests simultaneously. The optical test is still stuck at one bench instrument per measurement point. LightFinder is building the chip that changes that ratio.  The Optica GAMA audience saw the potential immediately. By the end of the Q&A, there were several offers of a packaging and automation partnership from the floor. Beyond CPO, the platform roadmap covers extended NIR and visible wavelengths—spectroscopy-on-a-chip for semiconductor process control, medical diagnostics, remote sensing, and industrial inspection. The same silicon photonic infrastructure being built for datacenters could produce sensing chips at a volume that rivals CPO itself. If you are working in photonic packaging, test, or sensing -- and you are not already talking to LightFinder -- now is the time. Diana Mojahed can be reached at diana@lightfindertech.com. WHY CO-PACKAGED OPTICS FAILED IN 2011 - AND WHY IT WON'T THIS TIME. At the Optica GAMA Meeting last week (June 2-3 2026), Bert Jan Offrein of IBM Research Zurich opened with a question that cuts to the heart of where photonics stands today: why, after IBM deployed co-packaged optics in a supercomputer back in 2011, did the industry walk away from it for a decade? The answer matters because we're back at the same junction. Follow the link below to watch the 21-minute presentation on the Optica YouTube channel. https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz.  In 2011, optics lost to a workaround. The ratio of communication to compute dropped from roughly one byte per flop to less than one hundredth. Electrical systems adapted, and the assembly overhead of optics - the lasers, modulators, drivers, alignment tolerances, fiber routing - simply wasn't worth it.  That trade-off no longer works. AI training and inference have reversed the pressure. We're back to multi-chip modules, back to bandwidth walls, and back to optics as the only credible path forward. But the overhead problem hasn't gone away.  Bert's argument is that solving it requires rethinking assembly, not just components. IBM's polymer waveguide approach - where light transitions adiabatically from a silicon or silicon nitride chip waveguide into a polymer matched to fiber mode size - enables 100 optical connections in a single flip-chip attach. That's the direction: optical connectivity that integrates into standard electrical assembly flows, is solder-reflow compatible, and is Telcordia-tested.  Further out, a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)-funded project is targeting 3D optical routing with 3-micron waveguide pitch, vertical vias, and chip-to-chip optical bonding through substrates - essentially replicating in the optical domain what the back-end-of-line does electrically.   Current mirror losses are around 1 dB and improving. The practical implication: the technology choices that will define the next generation of AI infrastructure won't be decided by peak performance specs. They'll be decided by who solves the assembly overhead at system level - not just the first-level package, but across the full board and chassis.  IBM Research is now operating as a collaborator rather than a licensor - open to partnerships that can bring these approaches to production. That shift in posture, from IP generator to system integrator, may matter as much as the technology itself.  Bert Jan Offrein presented at the Optica GAMA Meeting, June 2, 2026. Optica brings together the photonics community to accelerate exactly these kinds of industry-critical conversations. SABIC GRAND TOUR AND THE CHALLENGE OF REFLOW SOLDERING On our way to Belgium, Optica just visited 沙特基礎工業公司's Opto-Electronic Centre of Excellence in Bergen op Zoom, The Netherlands. We got the full tour with Gabrie Hoogland and Young Joon Choi to understand how new materials can solve one problem that catches optical designers off guard: reflow soldering. The interview is 30 minutes and is therefore available on YouTube.   JEDEC protocols run at 260°C, three passes. Most thermoplastic resins deform at that temperature. Most optical designers discover this at the packaging stage, not the design stage.  沙特基礎工業公司 developed Extem - a thermoplastic polyimide with a glass transition temperature of 280°C - specifically to close that gap. It survives reflow, can be injection moulded with 5nm surface roughness and sub-micron dimensional tolerances, and is capable of millions of parts per year. Three things stood out from the visit:  1. Alignment before reflow is now possible. Package your optics on the board first, then solder. That changes the economics for OSAT companies.  2. Epoxy is avoidable. Extem and Ultem can be metallised and self-aligned on a PCB via solder paste capillary action. No adhesive required.  3. Detachable connectors work. A demonstrator built with Tyndall National Institute showed 2.2 dB penalty over 40 make-and-break cycles using expanded beam microlens arrays. The loss came from the PIC design, not the lenses. So, if you are designing for co-packaged optics and have not checked your material's reflow compatibility, check now.  Interested in more information? Contact Gabrie Hoogland and tell them you saw the Optica interview. https://lnkd.in/g5z3kj-p

AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.
