WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

Watch this presentation on YouTube: https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN  Nick Psaila, formerly of OptoScribe and now leading co-packaged optics (CPO) development at Intel Foundry, delivered an excellent keynote at Optica Gamma Brussels 2026. His talk cut straight to the core problem: AI systems are no longer compute-limited, they are IO-limited, and copper interconnects are running out of road.  Psaila laid out why CPO is not a future technology but a present-tense supply chain emergency. With at least five one-gigawatt data centres expected online this year, and projections of over 100 million 1600G-equivalent optical links per facility, he warned the entire photonics supply chain, from PIC fabs to FAU manufacturers to assembly and metrology equipment providers, that volume investment is required now.  The talk then moved into advanced packaging as the critical enabler. Psaila argued that CPO is as much a packaging challenge as a photonics one, and that the industry needs to abandon artisan assembly processes in favour of wafer-level, high-throughput, JEDEC-qualified manufacturing compatible with heterogeneous integration and 3D stacking. He outlined Intel's packaging spectrum from EMIB to Foveros, and introduced their work on glass core substrates, including the first demonstration of a 24-layer glass core with embedded EMIB presented at ECTC the previous week. Glass core, he argued, solves the CTE mismatch problem that increasingly limits organic substrates at large panel sizes, and opens a path to integrating 3D waveguides directly into the substrate for in-package optical interconnects.  He closed with a long-range vision: panel-scale compute with an embedded optical connectivity matrix that routes signals from die-to-die to the external network within a single architecture.  The Q&A that followed was one of the more direct exchanges of the day. It has been edited out of this version. While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale.  In other news: Axonal Networks has been named a semifinalist in SEMI's Startups for Sustainable Semiconductors (S3) program, in the New Frontiers in Sustainable Computing category. 33 startups were selected for the virtual pitch event coming up this week on July 29-30, with 10-12 finalists advancing to pitch live at SEMICON West 2026 in San Francisco this October. The ministry framed the move as protecting national security and fulfilling non-proliferation obligations. Adam Piotrowski CEO of VIGO Photonics said, in comments carried by Reuters, that being placed on the list would not have a critical impact on its operations.  What this means:  This is a rare case of a named, publicly listed European photonics company being caught up directly in the EU-China sanctions exchange, rather than the larger defence and general semiconductor names that typically populate such lists. Even though Vigo Photonics has played down the operational impact, the listing signals that Beijing is willing to reach into the mid-cap photonics and infrared-sensing supply chain when retaliating against Brussels, a factor European photonics companies with any China-linked supply chain should now weigh in compliance and sourcing planning. That Beijing's response followed the EU's sanctions package by only a day, and matched its scale one-for-one, is widely read by trade analysts as a deliberate signal rather than a coincidence. However, China's own statement does not frame it that way.  Sources: CGTN; Reuters, via TradingView

LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

MUNICH-BASED LINQUE CLAIMS ENERGY REDUCTION of 25 times! In her last contribution as Optica Director of Technology for Optics and Optical Systems, my colleague Dr Olga Raz visited Linque in Munich.  Linque is doing something the silicon photonics world has talked about for years: a large-scale programmable photonic fabric that routes optical signals on-chip, with no optical-electrical-optical conversions anywhere in the path. Their RISE64 optical circuit switch debuted at OFC Conference this year and is now in customer validation, with hyperscalers and neo-clouds both at the table.  The number that gets attention is the company's claim of 25x better energy efficiency than conventional switches. The explanation is simple: in an electrical switch, most of the power goes into SerDes, error correction, and the lasers that regenerate the signal after each conversion. Remove the conversions and that power budget largely disappears.  Two things stood out from Olga's conversation with the team. First, they are positioning as a system integrator, not a chip vendor. When asked the build-to-be-acquired question, the answer was direct: "we are more of the acquirer." Second, their win at the IC Taiwan Grand Challenge in June, one of 11 selected from 209 startups across 38 countries, opens exactly the foundry and OSAT relationships a photonics company needs to scale.  The message Linque left us with applies to the whole industry: photonics reaching product stage in the data center is not a one-company story. It takes the full semiconductor value chain, from equipment makers and fabs to OSATs, chip designers and system integrators, moving at the speed this buildout demands.

META IS SELLING THE THING IT SAID IT NEEDED MORE OF Meta just admitted it has more AI compute than it knows what to do with. That single fact explains more about the state of the AI trade than any earnings call this quarter. On July 1, Bloomberg reported Meta is building a new unit, internally called Meta Compute, to sell its spare GPU capacity to outside customers. Two models are reportedly on the table: hosted access to Meta's own AI (including its new Muse Spark model, the AWS Bedrock playbook) or straight compute rental, the CoreWeave playbook. The unit is said to be run by infrastructure chief Santosh Janardhan, Superintelligence Labs lead Daniel Gross, and president Dina Powell McCormick.  The market's reaction tells you where the real anxiety sits. Meta stock jumped more than 10% that day, its best single session in five months, after a year in which the stock had fallen close to 15% and lagged the S&P 500. CoreWeave fell 10.8%. Nebius fell 12.4%. Meta has committed roughly $48 billion to renting GPUs from those two companies (a $21 billion CoreWeave deal, expanded in April, plus up to $27 billion with Nebius) because its own buildout couldn't keep pace with demand. If Meta suddenly has capacity to spare, either its infrastructure finally caught up, or the demand it built for never fully showed up.  That's the case Ed Zitron made to Ed Elson on this week's Prof G Markets. Meta still doesn't break out Meta AI or Llama revenue the way Google or OpenAI report their AI businesses, so reselling the leftover GPUs is the clearest return Meta can point to on its spending so far. Zitron's broader argument, laid out in his newsletter, is that most of the AI capex boom is really being justified by two customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, who account for the bulk of the industry's disclosed AI revenue. Strip them out and the rest of the "AI economy" thins out fast. As he posted on X the day the story broke: "We'll know we will hit the top when Meta sells compute to Anthropic."  Worth a counterpoint. SpaceX did something similar with xAI's Colossus 1 site, leasing capacity to Anthropic for roughly $1.25 billion a month and to Google for about $920 million a month, a pair of deals Bloomberg Intelligence estimates could be worth over $50 billion by 2028. Reselling spare capacity isn't automatically a distress signal. It can just as easily be a company admitting it over-built for a demand curve that hasn't arrived on schedule, and doing something rational with the surplus while it waits.  Which gets to the actual question worth asking: who is monetizing AI right now, in dollars, not narrative? NVIDIA's data center revenue hit $75.2 billion last quarter, up 92% year over year, at a 75% gross margin. Everyone downstream of Nvidia, Meta included, is still spending to find out if the bet pays off. https://lnkd.in/eSS7hccm

CANADA'S PHOTONICS MOMENT: WHY THE CPFC SPINOFF CHANGES EVERYTHING FOR WESTERN SEMICONDUCTOR SUPPLY CHAINS  The Canadian Photonics Fabrication Center is being spun off from the National Research Council Canada / Conseil national de recherches Canada as a private, independent foundry. That is not a minor administrative change. It is the moment a fragmented set of assets becomes a coherent supply chain.  I chatted with Paul Slaby, Managing Director of the Canadian Semiconductor Council, to understand what this actually means -- for the industry, for AI infrastructure, and for Western supply chain sovereignty.  A few things that struck me from this conversation: CPFC is now the only pure-play III-V foundry in North America. One of very few in the world. And it sits at the center of a cluster most people outside the industry have not yet mapped: Ciena's global R&D is managed out of Ottawa. 諾基亞's Optical Division is headquartered there. 捷普集團's co-packaged optics R&D facility is in Kanata. Inphos, building devices directly from CPFC output, is run by Joe Costello. This is not a collection of companies. It is a supply chain.  Paul is direct about what scaling this requires. Current CPFC assets are around half a billion dollars. He puts the investment needed to make this fully competitive -- from wafer capacity expansion to the R&D required to hit the yields AI applications demand from high-power indium phosphide -- somewhere between $5 billion and $10 billion. Large numbers. But not TSMC-scale silicon numbers. And the demand justification is there: the compound semiconductor market is forecast to grow from roughly $5 billion today to $30 billion within five years, driven almost entirely by AI data center optical interconnect requirements.  We also get into critical minerals. Canada holds the second-largest known reserves of the rare earth materials that III-V manufacturing depends on. The challenge is not what is in the ground. It is the decade-long timeline to bring a mine from discovery to production-ready output. That conversation on substrate supply and minerals sovereignty is one of the more frank exchanges in the interview.  If you are building partnerships in Canada, evaluating the Ottawa photonics cluster, or trying to understand where Western compound semiconductor capacity is actually coming from -- this is 15 minutes worth your time.

Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica, captured the challenge. He pointed out that quantum is currently moving at two separate speeds: academic research (measured in qubits) and industry reality (focused on scalable products). At the moment, they’re not aligned. While the science is forging ahead, the market is lagging in building the next-generation hardware needed to protect our critical infrastructure.  The timeline is tight. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Andrew Shields of Toshiba Europe UK thought a ten-year horizon was more realistic, but there’s great urgency nonetheless. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align. WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

Glass core, he argued, solves the CTE mismatch problem that increasingly limits organic substrates at large panel sizes, and opens a path to integrating 3D waveguides directly into the substrate for in-package optical interconnects.  He closed with a long-range vision: panel-scale compute with an embedded optical connectivity matrix that routes signals from die-to-die to the external network within a single architecture. While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. LEARN FROM Lumentum: BORROWED FROM SEMICONDUCTORS, BUILT FOR PHOTONICS: THE PACKAGING MOVE AI CONNECTIVITY NEEDS At Optica GAMA last week (June 2-3 2026), Matt Guzy, Advanced Packaging lead at Lumentum, did something rare: he showed us a working prototype and explained exactly how it was built. Watch his presentation here https://lnkd.in/gR9EyFYu.   Matt came to Lumentum after 21 years at Intel, where he worked on some of the earliest heterogeneous integration in client computing, including glass-core substrates and early chiplet stacking. He brought that background to a deceptively simple question: how do you package VCSELs with CMOS in a way that's actually manufacturable?  His answer was fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) - a process already running at volume in your smartphone. He dropped III-V VCSEL die, photodiodes, a TIA and a driver into a standard OSAT flow, following existing design rules without inventing a single new process step. The result: a compact optic engine 17.5 x 5.6mm - roughly the size of a tic-tac - capable of 12.8 Tb/s across 80 channels at 50 Gbps per channel, at under 2.5 pJ/bit, with bandwidth density above 1.5 Tb/s per millimeter.  The engineering choices were deliberate. He wanted to de-risk everything downstream - fibre integration, board validation, test - so he kept the assembly flow completely conventional. That discipline is what allowed the team to debut the package at OFC earlier this year.  Matt's broader point was equally sharp: the photonics industry doesn't need to repeat the painful early years of advanced semiconductor packaging. The yield learning, the process infrastructure, the OSAT ecosystem - it already exists. The opportunity is to design optical solutions around what works, rather than starting from scratch.  On standards, he was pragmatic: wait 12 to 18 months. The field is too fragmented today to standardise usefully. When two or three approaches pull ahead, standards will follow naturally and will actually mean something.  On the VCSEL vs. external laser question: he was clear-eyed. VCSELs are not a universal answer. They don't have the reach for scale-across applications. But for within-rack and rack-to-rack, they offer a lower-cost, lower-power, high-bandwidth option that doesn't require reinventing the supply chain.  The photonics community tends to treat packaging as a downstream problem. Matt's work suggests it should be the starting point.

WHY CO-PACKAGED OPTICS FAILED IN 2011 - AND WHY IT WON'T THIS TIME. At the Optica GAMA Meeting last week (June 2-3 2026), Bert Jan Offrein of IBM Research Zurich opened with a question that cuts to the heart of where photonics stands today: why, after IBM deployed co-packaged optics in a supercomputer back in 2011, did the industry walk away from it for a decade? The answer matters because we're back at the same junction. Follow the link below to watch the 21-minute presentation on the Optica YouTube channel. https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz.  In 2011, optics lost to a workaround. The ratio of communication to compute dropped from roughly one byte per flop to less than one hundredth. Electrical systems adapted, and the assembly overhead of optics - the lasers, modulators, drivers, alignment tolerances, fiber routing - simply wasn't worth it.  That trade-off no longer works. AI training and inference have reversed the pressure. We're back to multi-chip modules, back to bandwidth walls, and back to optics as the only credible path forward. But the overhead problem hasn't gone away.  Bert's argument is that solving it requires rethinking assembly, not just components. IBM's polymer waveguide approach - where light transitions adiabatically from a silicon or silicon nitride chip waveguide into a polymer matched to fiber mode size - enables 100 optical connections in a single flip-chip attach. That's the direction: optical connectivity that integrates into standard electrical assembly flows, is solder-reflow compatible, and is Telcordia-tested.  Further out, a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)-funded project is targeting 3D optical routing with 3-micron waveguide pitch, vertical vias, and chip-to-chip optical bonding through substrates - essentially replicating in the optical domain what the back-end-of-line does electrically.   Current mirror losses are around 1 dB and improving. The practical implication: the technology choices that will define the next generation of AI infrastructure won't be decided by peak performance specs. They'll be decided by who solves the assembly overhead at system level - not just the first-level package, but across the full board and chassis.  IBM Research is now operating as a collaborator rather than a licensor - open to partnerships that can bring these approaches to production. That shift in posture, from IP generator to system integrator, may matter as much as the technology itself.  Bert Jan Offrein presented at the Optica GAMA Meeting, June 2, 2026. Optica brings together the photonics community to accelerate exactly these kinds of industry-critical conversations. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A 50-POUND INSTRUMENT FITS ON A CHIP At the GAMA meeting in Brussels on June 3rd, Diana Mojahed, PhD, CEO of Optica Corporate member Lightfinder (based in Boston USA), closed the conference with something the room had not seen before. Lightfinder has built a chip-based optical spectrum analyzer on standard silicon photonics. No exotic materials. No moving parts. A device that fits in a small enclosure -- and delivers spectral resolution and bandwidth comparable to a Yokogawa OSA that weighs 50 pounds and costs tens of thousands of dollars per unit. The technology is a digital Fourier transform spectrometer: a cascade of Mach-Zehnder interferometers on a silicon photonic chip, using a single photodetector and a Fourier-domain encoding scheme to achieve very competitive resolution. Add one stage to the architecture, and you double your channel count -- an exponential scaling property that conventional dispersive spectrometers simply cannot match.  Why does this matter for our industry? Because co-packaged optics is heading toward volume production, and optical testing has not kept up. ATE companies can run 10,000 electronic tests simultaneously. The optical test is still stuck at one bench instrument per measurement point. LightFinder is building the chip that changes that ratio. Beyond CPO, the platform roadmap covers extended NIR and visible wavelengths—spectroscopy-on-a-chip for semiconductor process control, medical diagnostics, remote sensing, and industrial inspection. SABIC GRAND TOUR AND THE CHALLENGE OF REFLOW SOLDERING On our way to Belgium, Optica just visited 沙特基礎工業公司's Opto-Electronic Centre of Excellence in Bergen op Zoom, The Netherlands. We got the full tour with Gabrie Hoogland and Young Joon Choi to understand how new materials can solve one problem that catches optical designers off guard: reflow soldering. The interview is 30 minutes and is therefore available on YouTube.   JEDEC protocols run at 260°C, three passes. Most thermoplastic resins deform at that temperature. Most optical designers discover this at the packaging stage, not the design stage.  沙特基礎工業公司 developed Extem - a thermoplastic polyimide with a glass transition temperature of 280°C - specifically to close that gap. It survives reflow, can be injection moulded with 5nm surface roughness and sub-micron dimensional tolerances, and is capable of millions of parts per year. Three things stood out from the visit:  1. Alignment before reflow is now possible. Package your optics on the board first, then solder. That changes the economics for OSAT companies.  2. Epoxy is avoidable. Extem and Ultem can be metallised and self-aligned on a PCB via solder paste capillary action. No adhesive required.  3. Detachable connectors work. A demonstrator built with Tyndall National Institute showed 2.2 dB penalty over 40 make-and-break cycles using expanded beam microlens arrays. The loss came from the PIC design, not the lenses. So, if you are designing for co-packaged optics and have not checked your material's reflow compatibility, check now.  Interested in more information? AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Yunnan Chihong Zinc&Germanium Co., Ltd. scaling 6 inch substrates, San'An Optoelectronics Co., Ltd. running substrate to chip in a single house. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. The drones reshaping the front line in Ukraine are increasingly guided by a bare optical fibre paying out from a spool bolted to the airframe. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Nobody said who makes that fibre. So we went and found out.  Three things worth your attention.  It is not a bespoke defence product. It is ITU-T G.657.A2 bend-insensitive single-mode fibre, the same category developed for tight-radius routing in fibre-to-the-home. 1310 and 1550 nm, 250 micron coating, dynamic bend radius down to about 7.5 mm. The property that lets you turn a corner in an apartment block is the property that lets a drone unspool 30 km at speed without macrobend loss.  Fibre-guided drones and AI data centres are now bidding for the same product. Chinese cable went from 16 yuan per kilometre in January 2025 to 40 yuan in January 2026, according to Vedomosti via the Kyiv Post. Russia and Ukraine together consume an estimated 50 to 60 million fibre-kilometres a year. The upstream constraint appears to be preform capacity, which nobody expands quickly. A commodity telecom fibre has acquired a second, price-inelastic customer base, and our industry did not plan for that.  The specialist value has moved from the glass to the spool. Nobody draws fibre for drones. What matters is winding geometry, packing process, tension control and payout mechanics, because failures in flight are mechanical rather than optical. The firms doing that work well are small, European and American, and most of them are not yet part of our community. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale.  In other news: Axonal Networks has been named a semifinalist in SEMI's Startups for Sustainable Semiconductors (S3) program, in the New Frontiers in Sustainable Computing category. 33 startups were selected for the virtual pitch event coming up this week on July 29-30, with 10-12 finalists advancing to pitch live at SEMICON West 2026 in San Francisco this October. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

ILFA, a 45-year-old Hannover manufacturer with about 190 employees, builds complex PCBs for aerospace and defence, medical and industrial markets, including electro-optical boards, embedded component integration and fluid channel control, and holds 12 patent families. Citi is advising TTM on the STG transaction and Piper Sandler is advising STG.  What this means: The strategic value is in photonics-adjacent packaging. Electro-optical PCBs, waveguide embedding and miniaturised substrates for implantable photonic devices are exactly where optical functionality has to survive aggressive packaging constraints in medical and aerospace systems. "Chips don't float," TTM President and CEO Edwin Roks said in a recent Optica interview, pointing to the interconnect layer as the place where photonic and electronic systems finally have to coexist, with no tolerance margin in implantables or aerospace sensors. For European photonics, the deal is double-edged: it brings TTM investment and long-cycle demand into the region, while again moving specialist European manufacturing IP under US ownership. WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.
