WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

艾司摩爾 KEYNOTE: CALL FOR OPEN COLLABORATION IN PHOTONICS. At the Optica GAMA Meeting 2026 in Brussels last week (June 3rd), Henk Niesing , VP and Head of Technology EU/US at ASML delivered a special opening keynote on Day 2. The session opened with a direct announcement: next year's GAMA meeting will be hosted by 艾司摩爾 at its campus in Veldhoven, The Netherlands 12 – 13 May 2027. Mark that date in the calendar. You can watch the keynote presentation here: https://lnkd.in/eVTmiiT4  Niesing set the context quickly. AI is driving demand across the entire wafer production spectrum -- not just at the advanced EUV nodes that dominate headlines, but across the mainstream logic, analogue, power, photonics and sensor markets that represent the majority of wafers produced globally. That distinction matters for anyone in the room building components for the photonics supply chain.  The first half covered Moore's Law and packaging. Niesing argued that the scaling roadmap remains valid through 2042 but now requires a 16x improvement in compute per two-year cycle -- impossible on 2D scaling alone. The answer is heterogeneous 3D integration, and package sizes are growing as fast as devices are shrinking. ASML's response is a new lithography system with a 4x larger exposure field (52 by 68mm), designed specifically for the interposer layer where logic, memory and photonics converge. A full-wafer exposure capability is in development.  The second half addressed photonics patterning directly. Niesing walked through the challenges ASML hears from photonics customers: substrate diversity (InP still on 4-inch wafers), large topography of V-grooves, CD uniformity, pitch stability, and line-edge roughness. He presented ASML's holistic lithography approach -- combining scanner optimisation, computational lithography (OPC), and e-beam metrology -- with specific results: He identified resist selection and mask optimisation as two further levers the industry is underusing.  ASML's open collaboration request: any fab that measures both lithography parameters and optical propagation losses in the same process flow is a potential partner. That link is currently missing.  The Q&A included an exchange with Liron Gantz of NVIDIA, who noted that even indirect suppliers -- components going into the photonics supply chain -- should engage directly with ASML on the technology roadmap rather than waiting for requirements to filter down. Niesing agreed and called it exactly the kind of input 艾司摩爾 needs years in advance. Grab a coffee!

ELEPHANTS IN THE ROOM? We continue our deep-tech coverage of last week's Optica GAMA meeting in Brussels, with keynotes now on YouTube from PhotonHub https://lnkd.in/eyZubp7u, IBM https://lnkd.in/g56CA-mz and Intel Foundry https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN. These were honest engineering discussions about the real problems photonics companies face when they try to scale, not marketing spin. At recent meetings, also in Brussels, several of us have kept returning to one huge contradiction. We talk about European leadership, yet our substrates come largely from Asia, equipment suppliers often serve non-European customers first, and many European fabless PIC companies manufacture their chips outside Europe. If that is the supply chain we actually have, it is fair to ask whether funding more pilot lines for already mature technologies is the right move? Europe does not have a pilot-line problem. It has a commercialisation and industrial-scale manufacturing problem.  So on the morning of Day 2 at GAMA, before the ASML keynote, I walked the room to hear what people were actually saying. Ignazio Piacentini (IP Consulting), who works on assembly and test rather than devices, put it plainly. The story from day one was high-volume manufacturing, and it all turns on co-packaged optics and massive optical interconnect. The pull is coming from semiconductors, which are absorbing photonics as an enabling technology, and that is forcing the equipment makers to the next level. As he put it, ficonTEC is not moving from 1.0 to 2.0. It is heading to 3.0, and the rest of the equipment base will have to follow.  Then Andrea Rocchetto (EPHOS) raised the point that stayed with me. Two weeks ago the The Royal Society in London ran a photonics war game with three blocks. The West played IP as its strength. China played mass-scale volume manufacturing. South East Asia played its card in advanced packaging. The result was a clear win for China. Andrea would like to run the same game with an audience like this one, which is far more technical and informed. So would I. The rules and the final report are published on the Royal Society site so we hope to investigate further.   That is the elephant. We have the IP. We are short on the volume. The encouraging part is who was in the room. Bert Jan Offrein (IBM), Bernard Lee (SENKO), Sébastien Libon (ESA), Alexander Kessel (Intego), Lars Benesch (Photonics Supply and Services Partner) and others. And when it comes to semiconductor manufacturing at scale, Europe does have a world leader, which is why we opened Day 2 with a keynote and an announcement from Henk Niesing, head of technology at ASML. More coverage to follow.  Tell me where you think Europe should place its bets over the next five years.

INTEL KEYNOTE: Advanced packaging as the critical enabler. GRAB A COFFEE AND DON'T MISS THIS! Feeds from last week's GAMA meeting in Brussels have started all kinds of conversations. I am sure this will be another one. Watch this presentation on YouTube: https://lnkd.in/emWpCiUN  Nick Psaila, formerly of OptoScribe and now leading co-packaged optics (CPO) development at Intel Foundry, delivered an excellent keynote at Optica Gamma Brussels 2026. His talk cut straight to the core problem: AI systems are no longer compute-limited, they are IO-limited, and copper interconnects are running out of road.  Psaila laid out why CPO is not a future technology but a present-tense supply chain emergency. With at least five one-gigawatt data centres expected online this year, and projections of over 100 million 1600G-equivalent optical links per facility, he warned the entire photonics supply chain, from PIC fabs to FAU manufacturers to assembly and metrology equipment providers, that volume investment is required now.  The talk then moved into advanced packaging as the critical enabler. Psaila argued that CPO is as much a packaging challenge as a photonics one, and that the industry needs to abandon artisan assembly processes in favour of wafer-level, high-throughput, JEDEC-qualified manufacturing compatible with heterogeneous integration and 3D stacking. He outlined Intel's packaging spectrum from EMIB to Foveros, and introduced their work on glass core substrates, including the first demonstration of a 24-layer glass core with embedded EMIB presented at ECTC the previous week. Glass core, he argued, solves the CTE mismatch problem that increasingly limits organic substrates at large panel sizes, and opens a path to integrating 3D waveguides directly into the substrate for in-package optical interconnects.  He closed with a long-range vision: panel-scale compute with an embedded optical connectivity matrix that routes signals from die-to-die to the external network within a single architecture.  The Q&A that followed was one of the more direct exchanges of the day. It has been edited out of this version. Representatives from Opsydia, Ephos, and FEMTOPRINT SA each weighed in on their own approaches to direct laser writing for in-package waveguides, with Rolando Ferrini from FEMTOPRINT SA making the pointed argument that the industry cannot rely on a single supplier at this scale and that cross-licensing between European competitors may ultimately serve the market better than winner-takes-all competition. A voice-of-the-customer moment from Peter Kirkegaard cut through the noise: demand will be high enough that there is work for everyone. Further questions addressed polymer microoptics and their reliability constraints under reflow and TCB conditions, as well as how companies like Demcon Photonics are working to bring direct laser writing processes into foundry-compatible, high-volume manufacturing. For me, one of the best presentations in a long time. Agree?

While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe. That single fact explains more about the state of the AI trade than any earnings call this quarter. On July 1, Bloomberg reported Meta is building a new unit, internally called Meta Compute, to sell its spare GPU capacity to outside customers. Two models are reportedly on the table: hosted access to Meta's own AI (including its new Muse Spark model, the AWS Bedrock playbook) or straight compute rental, the CoreWeave playbook. If Meta suddenly has capacity to spare, either its infrastructure finally caught up, or the demand it built for never fully showed up. Meta still doesn't break out Meta AI or Llama revenue the way Google or OpenAI report their AI businesses, so reselling the leftover GPUs is the clearest return Meta can point to on its spending so far. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.
Excellent summary. Worth your time reading.

WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. WHEN THE DRONE TETHER IS MADE OF GLASS  I listened to a 英國廣播公司 Radio 4 documentary this week called Britain's Robot Army. One passing detail stopped me, and I think it belongs to our industry rather than to the defence press.  The drones reshaping the front line in Ukraine are increasingly guided by a bare optical fibre paying out from a spool bolted to the airframe. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Nobody said who makes that fibre. So we went and found out.  Three things worth your attention.  It is not a bespoke defence product. It is ITU-T G.657.A2 bend-insensitive single-mode fibre, the same category developed for tight-radius routing in fibre-to-the-home. 1310 and 1550 nm, 250 micron coating, dynamic bend radius down to about 7.5 mm. The property that lets you turn a corner in an apartment block is the property that lets a drone unspool 30 km at speed without macrobend loss.  Fibre-guided drones and AI data centres are now bidding for the same product. Chinese cable went from 16 yuan per kilometre in January 2025 to 40 yuan in January 2026, according to Vedomosti via the Kyiv Post. Russia and Ukraine together consume an estimated 50 to 60 million fibre-kilometres a year. The upstream constraint appears to be preform capacity, which nobody expands quickly. A commodity telecom fibre has acquired a second, price-inelastic customer base, and our industry did not plan for that.  The specialist value has moved from the glass to the spool. Nobody draws fibre for drones. What matters is winding geometry, packing process, tension control and payout mechanics, because failures in flight are mechanical rather than optical. The firms doing that work well are small, European and American, and most of them are not yet part of our community. CALLING Optica CORPORATE MEMBERS: THE NEXT-GENERATION RGB LIGHT ENGINE is ready for testing. Details below. I spent a day in  #Enschede, The Netherlands with Tim Tiek, CEO of Brilliance RGB, witnessing a small team turn silicon nitride photonic integrated circuits into a full RGB light engine, small enough for AR glasses and thin enough for a car dashboard. PICs have lived mainly in datacom and telecom for two decades. Brilliance RGB, founded about three years ago, is pushing the same platform into a market with far higher volume: visible light for AR/VR eyewear, automotive displays, and industrial sensing. The chip integrates lasers, waveguides, and sensors onto a single wafer-scale silicon nitride platform, replacing the lenses, prisms, and discrete lasers that make traditional RGB projectors (including IMAX) bulky and expensive.  Why silicon nitride specifically? It couples laser light into waveguides with very high efficiency, which matters most for eyewear: a glasses form factor with a battery that has to last a full day of projection lives or dies on power efficiency. Tim's case for laser displays over micro-LED comes down to full colour, wide field of view, and outdoor brightness, though he's clear micro-LED still wins for simple monochrome use cases like sport glasses.  The automotive angle is just as concrete. Today's heads-up displays run on LCOS panels behind the steering wheel, bulky and lossy by design. Brilliance's approach could shrink that by a factor of ten while cutting cooling overhead, and the same chip architecture could support ground projection as self-driving cars start signalling turns and warnings to pedestrians. Tim's team is already in conversations with Tier 1 suppliers and OEMs on that.  Credibility is building fast for a three-year-old company. Google's Bernard Kress, speaking at the recent Optica summit at 康寧公司, has publicly called PICs a promising technology for next-gen AR/VR goggles, and Brilliance RGB is active in the growing laser-display ecosystem, alongside more than 40 companies now working on laser projection as a category. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale.  In other news: Axonal Networks has been named a semifinalist in SEMI's Startups for Sustainable Semiconductors (S3) program, in the New Frontiers in Sustainable Computing category. 33 startups were selected for the virtual pitch event coming up this week on July 29-30, with 10-12 finalists advancing to pitch live at SEMICON West 2026 in San Francisco this October. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

Greater Glasgow was recently ranked the fifth most important quantum cluster in the world, and first globally for its role as a sector hub. That’s an incredible achievement for the UK, and a massive nod to Scotland's deep-tech ecosystem.  This week I’ve been following discussions at Optica's Quantum 2.0 Conference in Glasgow (15–18 June) where one of the themes has been the race to translate raw R&D into practical, commercial applications.  Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica, captured the challenge. He pointed out that quantum is currently moving at two separate speeds: academic research (measured in qubits) and industry reality (focused on scalable products). At the moment, they’re not aligned. While the science is forging ahead, the market is lagging in building the next-generation hardware needed to protect our critical infrastructure.  The timeline is tight. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Andrew Shields of Toshiba Europe UK thought a ten-year horizon was more realistic, but there’s great urgency nonetheless. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. Scottish space company Craft Prospect is already working on using satellites to facilitate Quantum Key Distribution from space – a vital step in scaling these networks from regional to global models.  For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align.  This ties in perfectly with the work being done by QURECA, which was recently highlighted at the Quantum ARC event in Glasgow. That marked the launch of a new report titled ‘Inside Scotland’s Quantum Ecosystem’ – yet another reminder of the country’s key role in the quantum race.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

艾司摩爾 KEYNOTE: CALL FOR OPEN COLLABORATION IN PHOTONICS. At the Optica GAMA Meeting 2026 in Brussels last week (June 3rd), Henk Niesing , VP and Head of Technology EU/US at ASML delivered a special opening keynote on Day 2. The session opened with a direct announcement: next year's GAMA meeting will be hosted by 艾司摩爾 at its campus in Veldhoven, The Netherlands 12 – 13 May 2027. Mark that date in the calendar. You can watch the keynote presentation here: https://lnkd.in/eVTmiiT4  Niesing set the context quickly. AI is driving demand across the entire wafer production spectrum -- not just at the advanced EUV nodes that dominate headlines, but across the mainstream logic, analogue, power, photonics and sensor markets that represent the majority of wafers produced globally. That distinction matters for anyone in the room building components for the photonics supply chain.  The first half covered Moore's Law and packaging. Niesing argued that the scaling roadmap remains valid through 2042 but now requires a 16x improvement in compute per two-year cycle -- impossible on 2D scaling alone. The answer is heterogeneous 3D integration, and package sizes are growing as fast as devices are shrinking. ASML's response is a new lithography system with a 4x larger exposure field (52 by 68mm), designed specifically for the interposer layer where logic, memory and photonics converge. A full-wafer exposure capability is in development.  The second half addressed photonics patterning directly. Niesing walked through the challenges ASML hears from photonics customers: substrate diversity (InP still on 4-inch wafers), large topography of V-grooves, CD uniformity, pitch stability, and line-edge roughness. He presented ASML's holistic lithography approach -- combining scanner optimisation, computational lithography (OPC), and e-beam metrology -- with specific results: He identified resist selection and mask optimisation as two further levers the industry is underusing.  ASML's open collaboration request: any fab that measures both lithography parameters and optical propagation losses in the same process flow is a potential partner. That link is currently missing.  The Q&A included an exchange with Liron Gantz of NVIDIA, who noted that even indirect suppliers -- components going into the photonics supply chain -- should engage directly with ASML on the technology roadmap rather than waiting for requirements to filter down. Niesing agreed and called it exactly the kind of input 艾司摩爾 needs years in advance. Grab a coffee!

Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale. ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

META IS SELLING THE THING IT SAID IT NEEDED MORE OF Meta just admitted it has more AI compute than it knows what to do with. That single fact explains more about the state of the AI trade than any earnings call this quarter. On July 1, Bloomberg reported Meta is building a new unit, internally called Meta Compute, to sell its spare GPU capacity to outside customers. Two models are reportedly on the table: hosted access to Meta's own AI (including its new Muse Spark model, the AWS Bedrock playbook) or straight compute rental, the CoreWeave playbook. The unit is said to be run by infrastructure chief Santosh Janardhan, Superintelligence Labs lead Daniel Gross, and president Dina Powell McCormick.  The market's reaction tells you where the real anxiety sits. Meta stock jumped more than 10% that day, its best single session in five months, after a year in which the stock had fallen close to 15% and lagged the S&P 500. CoreWeave fell 10.8%. Nebius fell 12.4%. Meta has committed roughly $48 billion to renting GPUs from those two companies (a $21 billion CoreWeave deal, expanded in April, plus up to $27 billion with Nebius) because its own buildout couldn't keep pace with demand. If Meta suddenly has capacity to spare, either its infrastructure finally caught up, or the demand it built for never fully showed up.  That's the case Ed Zitron made to Ed Elson on this week's Prof G Markets. Meta still doesn't break out Meta AI or Llama revenue the way Google or OpenAI report their AI businesses, so reselling the leftover GPUs is the clearest return Meta can point to on its spending so far. Zitron's broader argument, laid out in his newsletter, is that most of the AI capex boom is really being justified by two customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, who account for the bulk of the industry's disclosed AI revenue. Strip them out and the rest of the "AI economy" thins out fast. As he posted on X the day the story broke: "We'll know we will hit the top when Meta sells compute to Anthropic."  Worth a counterpoint. SpaceX did something similar with xAI's Colossus 1 site, leasing capacity to Anthropic for roughly $1.25 billion a month and to Google for about $920 million a month, a pair of deals Bloomberg Intelligence estimates could be worth over $50 billion by 2028. Reselling spare capacity isn't automatically a distress signal. It can just as easily be a company admitting it over-built for a demand curve that hasn't arrived on schedule, and doing something rational with the surplus while it waits.  Which gets to the actual question worth asking: who is monetizing AI right now, in dollars, not narrative? NVIDIA's data center revenue hit $75.2 billion last quarter, up 92% year over year, at a 75% gross margin. Greater Glasgow was recently ranked the fifth most important quantum cluster in the world, and first globally for its role as a sector hub. That’s an incredible achievement for the UK, and a massive nod to Scotland's deep-tech ecosystem.  This week I’ve been following discussions at Optica's Quantum 2.0 Conference in Glasgow (15–18 June) where one of the themes has been the race to translate raw R&D into practical, commercial applications.  Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica, captured the challenge. He pointed out that quantum is currently moving at two separate speeds: academic research (measured in qubits) and industry reality (focused on scalable products). At the moment, they’re not aligned. While the science is forging ahead, the market is lagging in building the next-generation hardware needed to protect our critical infrastructure.  The timeline is tight. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Andrew Shields of Toshiba Europe UK thought a ten-year horizon was more realistic, but there’s great urgency nonetheless. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. Scottish space company Craft Prospect is already working on using satellites to facilitate Quantum Key Distribution from space – a vital step in scaling these networks from regional to global models.  For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align.  This ties in perfectly with the work being done by QURECA, which was recently highlighted at the Quantum ARC event in Glasgow. That marked the launch of a new report titled ‘Inside Scotland’s Quantum Ecosystem’ – yet another reminder of the country’s key role in the quantum race.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

WILL QUANTUM SCALE OR FAIL? That was the question running through my opening remarks on Tuesday at the Optica Quantum 2.0 and Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow this week, before an audience of 750 and a record 61 exhibition booths. Here is what I wanted everyone in the room to take away. Watch the video below to see the clip. Quantum runs on two clocks. One is R&D, measured in qubits and bit error rate. The other is commercial, measured in investment, manufacturing capacity and speed to market. These two clocks report to different stakeholders, and the whole point of bringing the research community and the industrial community into the same building is to make them tick together.  Why now? Because the money has changed character. Three of the world's largest economies are treating quantum as critical infrastructure with taxpayer money behind it: roughly 2bn USD in the US alongside IBM's 11bn commitment to manufacture quantum at home, 11bn in the EU Quantum Act over the next five years, and 2bn GBP in the UK. On the private side, Quantinuum is heading to an IPO near 1.7bn USD and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) raised 260m GBP, the largest round ever for a European quantum company.  The technical progress is real, too. We are seeing error correction progress quickly, including demonstrations of correcting 40 logical qubits out of 90. But the most important signal came from two companies I spoke to before the event. QuiX Quantum in Enschede is building photonic quantum chips designed so the hardware naturally fits the customer's algorithm, particularly for quantum chemistry. Jelmer Renema, CSO: people are lining up at the door. Imran Khan, Managing Director of German CVQKD company, KEEQuant, building integrated photonics for quantum key distribution, put it more bluntly: the threat is real now, telecom operators need these chips in volume today, and we cannot wait for the threat to materialise. They have already run a 900km carrier-grade link between Berlin and Bonn, delivered as keys-as-a-service.  That is the shift. A few years ago, quantum capital was blue-sky money. Today, every investor in the room is asking the same question: if I put money in, will you be in production in three years?  The technology is ready. The capital is ready. What remains is execution. We either scale or we fail.  By Thursday, if you were in Glasgow, do not tell me the summit was interesting. Tell me you connected with three real leads, and that at least one came from the other side of the aisle. Comments and suggestions welcome below. If you are in Glasgow, please say hello and connect with others (including me).   Next stop, Copenhagen, 7 to 10 June 2027. Onward!

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. Lutz is also a board member of Light Conversion in Lithuania and works with Marvel Fusion in Germany, so he speaks from inside the companies, not only from the policy room.  What is working in Europe: Europe leads the world in photonics, and 80% of that leadership has nothing to do with semiconductors. Ultrashort-pulse lasers, laser cutting, and lens making. This is core to our strategic autonomy, and it is easy to forget when every headline is about chips. Chips Joint Undertaking matters, but photonics is far bigger than its semiconductor slice. The base is strong too: a deep university landscape, a Photonics21 community of 4,500 members, mostly SMEs, and a venture capital environment that has genuinely improved.  What is too slow: Scaling. In Lutz's words, "we are good at inventing things and building prototypes, we struggle with scaling." The gap is specific. Companies can raise early money, and once they pass roughly 50 million Euro in revenue a later-stage ecosystem funds them. In between, there is a hole. The European Commission sees it. But the problem is far from being solved. And the real constraint is risk appetite, not cost. Automation has reduced the role of labour costs. What holds us back is the risk tolerance of industry, society, and policymakers.  Two examples he keeps returning to: Lithuania got it right. Vilnius matched R&D with manufacturing and valorisation in the same country, built on a strong talent pipeline. Light Conversion grew into the world's most important femtosecond laser maker from that base. Germany is where the next bet sits. Marvel Fusion is now the leader in laser fusion worldwide. Lutz expects first-of-a-kind and early commercial reactors in the 2030s, a complement to renewables and a route to energy independence, since Europe already has the resources fusion needs.  His warning is blunt. We let semiconductor manufacturing disappear, and regaining that autonomy is now enormously expensive. In photonics, we still lead, so holding the line costs far less than rebuilding it would. "Otherwise it costs us 10 times more to reestablish that, if it is possible at all." There was a sense of urgency in the room this year. We are still ahead. Now we have to act like it. Agree? Comment below.

While  #ASML's share price hit a new record, the Netherlands has more crucial technology to offer than litho tools from Veldhoven.  That is why the Dutch cabinet is planning to better shield vital technology from foreign takeovers. AI, biotechnology, and the development of advanced materials and sensor technology will soon be added to the list of 'sensitive' applications, to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands and being used for espionage or sabotage.  On Monday, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Heleen Herbert (CDA) announced that she is adding six new technologies to the Security Screening of Investments, Mergers and Acquisitions Act ( #Vifo). This act has protected quantum computers, photonics, semiconductors, chip equipment and other technologies with potential military applications since 2023. Other categories to be added to the 'sensitive' Vifo list from 2027: nanotechnology, genetic modification, location technology and nuclear applications for medical use.  The Vifo Act can be applied retroactively to 2020. That date does not reach quite far enough to reverse the Chinese takeover of chipmaker  #Nexperia (2019). When the Ministry of Economic Affairs decided in September 2025 to intervene at Nexperia — because the company was seeking to transfer vital knowledge and expertise to China — caretaker minister Vincent Karremans did so on the basis of a different law. He fell back on the obscure Availability of Goods Act, conceived in the 1950s but never previously used. The law prevents major changes within a company from being implemented without the minister's approval.  The Netherlands is becoming increasingly aware that foreign takeovers can cause problems, as shown recently when State Secretary Willemijn Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty, D66) blocked the proposed takeover of  #DigiD operator  #Solvinity by American firm  #Kyndryl. AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.
