JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Yunnan Chihong Zinc&Germanium Co., Ltd. scaling 6 inch substrates, San'An Optoelectronics Co., Ltd. running substrate to chip in a single house. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. WHEN THE DRONE TETHER IS MADE OF GLASS  I listened to a 英國廣播公司 Radio 4 documentary this week called Britain's Robot Army. One passing detail stopped me, and I think it belongs to our industry rather than to the defence press.  The drones reshaping the front line in Ukraine are increasingly guided by a bare optical fibre paying out from a spool bolted to the airframe. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Nobody said who makes that fibre. So we went and found out.  Three things worth your attention.  It is not a bespoke defence product. It is ITU-T G.657.A2 bend-insensitive single-mode fibre, the same category developed for tight-radius routing in fibre-to-the-home. 1310 and 1550 nm, 250 micron coating, dynamic bend radius down to about 7.5 mm. The property that lets you turn a corner in an apartment block is the property that lets a drone unspool 30 km at speed without macrobend loss.  Fibre-guided drones and AI data centres are now bidding for the same product. Chinese cable went from 16 yuan per kilometre in January 2025 to 40 yuan in January 2026, according to Vedomosti via the Kyiv Post. Russia and Ukraine together consume an estimated 50 to 60 million fibre-kilometres a year. The upstream constraint appears to be preform capacity, which nobody expands quickly. A commodity telecom fibre has acquired a second, price-inelastic customer base, and our industry did not plan for that.  The specialist value has moved from the glass to the spool. Nobody draws fibre for drones. What matters is winding geometry, packing process, tension control and payout mechanics, because failures in flight are mechanical rather than optical. The firms doing that work well are small, European and American, and most of them are not yet part of our community. GlobalFoundries is the outlier and the one that leaves room for everyone else, selling bespoke, standards-compliant optical engines that customers package themselves.  Two things I would take from all this.  Energy is becoming the unit of account. Samsung's public numbers run from roughly 10 picojoules per bit today, to 5, to 2 at interposer integration. PROMISED UPDATE: Japanese chip plants restart after Kumamoto earthquake Semiconductor facilities in the Kumamoto area began restarting within days of Tuesday's magnitude 7.1 earthquake. Renesas Electronics resumed production at its Nishiki plant on Wednesday night after confirming clean room integrity and expects its Kawashiri plant in Kumamoto city, in operation since 1970, to restart on 5 August despite wall cracks and water leaks. Toshiya Suzuki of Omdia [OPTICA CORPORATE MEMBER] attributed the speed of recovery to seismic isolation in fab construction and to business continuity planning.  What this means: The recovery time is the real story. A decade ago, the same region took roughly three months to restore chip production; this time, most plants are back up and running within a week, and Sony expects pre-quake output by mid-August. Geographic concentration risk in Kumamoto has not gone away, but the cost of that risk has fallen sharply, which weakens one argument European policymakers have used for onshoring. Suppliers of contamination-sensitive optical and metrology equipment should note the specific failure mode reported by TSMC suppliers: impurity accumulation in process equipment that requires cleaning or replacement, rather than structural damage. AT LAST! - PHOTONICS MOVES UP IN THE UNITED KINGDOM. The UK just quietly redefined what counts as a semiconductor company. Photonics is now inside the line.  The UK Dept for Science, Industry and Tech (DSIT) has published the 2026 UK Semiconductor Sectoral Analysis. Mainstream media will headline these numbers: 703 companies, £10.6bn in revenue, £7.5bn GVA, 16,350 direct jobs. But while researching for the panels at 2026 Optica's GPEF in Malaga, I discovered this interesting detail in endnote ix.  "Companies designing, developing or manufacturing photonic integrated circuits (PICs) were classified as dedicated." In the 2024 baseline, a PIC company sat in the diversified bucket. A company that touches semiconductors.   In 2026 it is a semiconductor company BY DEFINITION. That matters, because the dedicated cohort is what DSIT measures, funds and calibrates policy against.  The rest of the report is consistent with that shift:  Photonic IC design and fabrication took 11% of new UK semiconductor research funding in 2024 and 2025. 4th largest category.  Integrated photonics is named as a UK strength, with three geographies attached: Southampton, Glasgow, Northern Ireland.  The top UK assignee of granted US semiconductor patents in 2024 and 2025 is ROCKLEY PHOTONICS LIMITED. That's above Arm.  And the argument the report makes for why: photonic interconnect is part of the AI compute stack "where the UK can compete on capability rather than capital intensity." CALLING Optica CORPORATE MEMBERS: THE NEXT-GENERATION RGB LIGHT ENGINE is ready for testing. Details below. I spent a day in  #Enschede, The Netherlands with Tim Tiek, CEO of Brilliance RGB, witnessing a small team turn silicon nitride photonic integrated circuits into a full RGB light engine, small enough for AR glasses and thin enough for a car dashboard. PICs have lived mainly in datacom and telecom for two decades. Brilliance RGB, founded about three years ago, is pushing the same platform into a market with far higher volume: visible light for AR/VR eyewear, automotive displays, and industrial sensing. The chip integrates lasers, waveguides, and sensors onto a single wafer-scale silicon nitride platform, replacing the lenses, prisms, and discrete lasers that make traditional RGB projectors (including IMAX) bulky and expensive.  Why silicon nitride specifically? It couples laser light into waveguides with very high efficiency, which matters most for eyewear: a glasses form factor with a battery that has to last a full day of projection lives or dies on power efficiency. Tim's case for laser displays over micro-LED comes down to full colour, wide field of view, and outdoor brightness, though he's clear micro-LED still wins for simple monochrome use cases like sport glasses.  The automotive angle is just as concrete. Today's heads-up displays run on LCOS panels behind the steering wheel, bulky and lossy by design. Brilliance's approach could shrink that by a factor of ten while cutting cooling overhead, and the same chip architecture could support ground projection as self-driving cars start signalling turns and warnings to pedestrians. Tim's team is already in conversations with Tier 1 suppliers and OEMs on that.  Credibility is building fast for a three-year-old company. Google's Bernard Kress, speaking at the recent Optica summit at 康寧公司, has publicly called PICs a promising technology for next-gen AR/VR goggles, and Brilliance RGB is active in the growing laser-display ecosystem, alongside more than 40 companies now working on laser projection as a category. Brilliance has working prototypes, packaged chips, and active design studies with customers. The next test is scale: moving from hundreds of units today to the volumes consumer electronics and automotive demand, using local foundry and packaging partners in Enschede now, with eight-inch foundry partners lined up for high-volume production.  If you're an Optica corporate member and want to test Brilliance's RGB light engine yourself, reach out to Tim Tiek directly by mentioning this LinkedIn post, or contact me at Optica for an introduction.

AI IS HITTING A WALL. Axonal Networks THINKS PHOTONS CAN FIX IT. I sat down with David Rolston, Founder and CEO of Axonal Networks, at his HQ and labs in Montreal. Rolston previously built Reflex Photonics before founding Axonal in 2021 with a different starting point. Instead of designing a device and working up, he started with the architecture, then built the devices to match it. The core problem: today's AI switch fabrics move data as electrons through copper, and at scale that means huge power draw, crosstalk, and signal degradation that require heavy correction circuitry just to keep ones and zeros intact. Rolston's answer is Digital Photonics, doing the actual switching logic in silicon photonics rather than electronics.  The building block is a micro-ring modulator, used to construct optical NAND and NOR gates. Micro-rings are highly sensitive to temperature and process variation, so Axonal built a thermal feedback stabilization circuit, a small transistor-based auto-calibrating loop, to keep the rings locked to the laser input.  Three products come out of this: paraNu, a high-channel-count optical transceiver (scaling from 8 to 32 channels) paraLITE, optical logic gates for small digital controllers, comparators, and PRBS generators paraDOX, the long-term goal: a parallel digital optical cross-connect switch fabric targeting thousands of ports, keeping electron movement confined to within a micron inside each logic gate to eliminate EMI and crosstalk  The scale argument is the headline number: Rolston says a 200,000-GPU cluster today needs roughly 8,000 switches, and Axonal's architecture is aimed at cutting that to around 150, while staying compatible with existing Ethernet, InfiniBand, leaf-spine designs so operators wouldn't need to rearchitect around it.  On manufacturing, Axonal isn't building its own fab. Rolston is leaning on Montreal's photonics ecosystem, four area universities, hubs like C2MI and INO, and contract manufacturers including 天弘 and 新美亞 for packaging at production scale. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

META IS SELLING THE THING IT SAID IT NEEDED MORE OF Meta just admitted it has more AI compute than it knows what to do with. That single fact explains more about the state of the AI trade than any earnings call this quarter. On July 1, Bloomberg reported Meta is building a new unit, internally called Meta Compute, to sell its spare GPU capacity to outside customers. Two models are reportedly on the table: hosted access to Meta's own AI (including its new Muse Spark model, the AWS Bedrock playbook) or straight compute rental, the CoreWeave playbook. The unit is said to be run by infrastructure chief Santosh Janardhan, Superintelligence Labs lead Daniel Gross, and president Dina Powell McCormick.  The market's reaction tells you where the real anxiety sits. Meta stock jumped more than 10% that day, its best single session in five months, after a year in which the stock had fallen close to 15% and lagged the S&P 500. CoreWeave fell 10.8%. Nebius fell 12.4%. Meta has committed roughly $48 billion to renting GPUs from those two companies (a $21 billion CoreWeave deal, expanded in April, plus up to $27 billion with Nebius) because its own buildout couldn't keep pace with demand. If Meta suddenly has capacity to spare, either its infrastructure finally caught up, or the demand it built for never fully showed up.  That's the case Ed Zitron made to Ed Elson on this week's Prof G Markets. Meta still doesn't break out Meta AI or Llama revenue the way Google or OpenAI report their AI businesses, so reselling the leftover GPUs is the clearest return Meta can point to on its spending so far. Zitron's broader argument, laid out in his newsletter, is that most of the AI capex boom is really being justified by two customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, who account for the bulk of the industry's disclosed AI revenue. Strip them out and the rest of the "AI economy" thins out fast. As he posted on X the day the story broke: "We'll know we will hit the top when Meta sells compute to Anthropic."  Worth a counterpoint. SpaceX did something similar with xAI's Colossus 1 site, leasing capacity to Anthropic for roughly $1.25 billion a month and to Google for about $920 million a month, a pair of deals Bloomberg Intelligence estimates could be worth over $50 billion by 2028. Reselling spare capacity isn't automatically a distress signal. It can just as easily be a company admitting it over-built for a demand curve that hasn't arrived on schedule, and doing something rational with the surplus while it waits.  Which gets to the actual question worth asking: who is monetizing AI right now, in dollars, not narrative? Greater Glasgow was recently ranked the fifth most important quantum cluster in the world, and first globally for its role as a sector hub. That’s an incredible achievement for the UK, and a massive nod to Scotland's deep-tech ecosystem. He pointed out that quantum is currently moving at two separate speeds: academic research (measured in qubits) and industry reality (focused on scalable products). At the moment, they’re not aligned. While the science is forging ahead, the market is lagging in building the next-generation hardware needed to protect our critical infrastructure.  The timeline is tight. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Andrew Shields of Toshiba Europe UK thought a ten-year horizon was more realistic, but there’s great urgency nonetheless. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align. WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

IN PHOTONICS, EUROPE STILL LEADS. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER WE KEEP IT. I caught up with Lutz Aschke, President of Photonics21, at the annual meeting in Brussels this week. AN AI AGENT JUST LEARNED TO FIX A LASER LOCK. WHY THIS IS A PHOTONICS STORY, NOT THE MICROSCOPES. Anthropic opened a research preview last week of the Model Hardware Standard, MHS. It gives an AI agent one common way to discover and operate physical instruments. Each device gets a driver with read and write primitives, plus plain language tags describing what it does and the safety limits it must not cross.   The coverage went to pipetting robots and microscopes. The result our industry should read came from QuEra Computing Inc..   QuEra builds neutral-atom quantum computers that stop when a laser loses lock. Four specialists had already spent two to three weeks writing a recovery script by hand. Working through MHS, Claude ran its own experiments on a dedicated laser testbed inside engineer-set limits, then wrote conventional software the engineers could inspect and sign off.   Relock went from 150 seconds at 58 percent success to 6 seconds at 96 percent. In a blind test it recovered the lock in 695 of 700 trials across seven fault types, with no false reports of success. Human specialists needed 5 to 10 minutes.   So is this only useful for prototyping?   A 300mm fab does not have the problem MHS solves. Production equipment has spoken SECS/GEM since the 1980s and EDA since the 2000s. That layer is settled and governed.   Photonics hurts downstream of the fab, namely n test, alignment and packaging. High mix, multi-vendor, script-driven. Tunable lasers, power meters, polarisation controllers, piezo stages and thermal chucks from six suppliers, glued together with custom code that gets rewritten for every product. 美國卡內基美隆大學 went from raw equipment to a finished measurement curve in eight hours using MHS, against several weeks for conventional vendor setup. That is our problem, not the fab's.   For a scaler, the value is the artefact, not the agent. Claude never sat in QuEra's control loop. It developed the routine and handed over deterministic code. Agent in process development, script in production. That is a shape quality and audit can live with.   What it does not fix: an agent will not make a piezo stage settle faster. Alignment time per die is mechanics and physics.   Now look at who is building MHS support. Amazon Web Services (AWS), Danaher, Doosan Robotics, QIAGEN, Tecan, Universal Robots, Hugging FaceFace, Raspberry Pi Foundation. Life sciences and robotics company. Not one photonics test or alignment vendor. That is strange. Why not?    Our benches are already full of programmable instruments. SCPI and VISA have been standard for decades. An MHS driver for a tunable laser or an alignment stage is a smaller job than for most biology hardware, and the payoff is larger because our mix is worse.   My read is that whoever in photonics writes the first good drivers will shape what the rest of us inherit. Video below from Anthropic. https://lnkd.in/ebfsTqUC

Xanadu, Project OPTIMISM LANDS AND ITS IMPACT ON THE GLOBAL QUANTUM SUPPLY CHAIN  In June, at the Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, Xanadu's Chief Operating Officer told the room the company was setting up a 160,000 square foot facility in Toronto to bring heterogeneous integration in-house. On Thursday, August 27th, they got a loan, not a grant, with repayments set as a percentage of future revenue.   Rafal Janik was keynoting our photonic quantum computing session, the first time Xanadu had spoken at an Optica industry event. Asked from the floor in the clip below about supply chain concentration in thin film lithium niobate, he gave an answer that reads differently now:   "Global supply chains are absolutely an issue. The really good thing is that quantum has been identified as a strategic priority for pretty much every single government in the world, so everybody's trying to onshore a lot of these materials now."   Thursday was that sentence turning into a building.   The facility is called Inception. A former Campbell's soup plant in Etobicoke, anchoring a CAD 893 million project, 275 technical jobs. Cleanrooms for heterogeneous integration, round the clock wafer level test, a systems integration centre where modules are verified before they go into racks.   That is a packaging and assembly plant. The quantum computer is the customer.   Janik was explicit in Glasgow about why it has to exist. Xanadu runs three material stacks, silicon nitride, thin film lithium niobate and III-V, and building them separately is no longer sufficient. They have to be integrated. Heterogeneous integration is the bottleneck, and it is a packaging problem before it is a physics problem.   Now look at who supplies the tools. ASMPT Ltd, Bluefors, DISCO, EV Group, ficonTECTEC and 旺矽科技股份有限公司. Singapore, Finland, Japan, Austria, Germany, Taiwan. Three of the six are European. Canada is buying supply chain sovereignty, and a large part of that supply chain is European.   I do not say that as criticism. It is the honest shape of our industry. Nobody sets up a photonic packaging line alone, because the equipment base is thin and spread across firms that have each spent decades becoming very good at one step.   The caveat matters. A packaging plant does not solve fault tolerance. Heterogeneous integration at production yield is unproven at this scale, and Inception is announced rather than running. My read is that the durable asset is the line itself. If photonic fault tolerance takes longer than its advocates expect, Canada still owns a general-purpose photonic integration capability. Those are scarce, and they are useful to AI hardware, telecom and sensing, whatever happens to qubits.   For European photonics companies the lesson is not to envy the cheque. When a government funds quantum manufacturing, a large share of it lands on equipment vendors. Europe is strong there. That is a position to defend deliberately, not one to assume will hold.

David Huang's presentation (15 min) from the Optica OIM on Photonics in Ophthalmology & Vision Care August 25th is worth a wider audience. OCT did not win because it was the best physics. It won because someone could bill for it.   David Huang co-invented optical coherence tomography, and in this clip he tells the origin story himself. It began as close to a pure physics experiment, using light to measure time of flight and see below a surface, in Professor Fujimoto's lab at MIT while he was a PhD student.   Then the dates.   First publication, 1991. First patent, 1994. First FDA cleared system, from Humphrey Zeiss, 1996. First CPT code, meaning a clinician could finally charge for the scan, 1997.   Six years from paper to reimbursement.   Adoption followed the billing code. Once the scan could be paid for, the revenue funded better instruments, which widened the clinical case, which justified better reimbursement. OCT did not even have that code to itself. It shared 92135 with retinal thickness analysers, slit scan tomography and scanning laser polarimetry, and took the market on depth resolution.   Huang is unusually direct about the rest of it. Regulatory steps were easier then, the founders did everything right, and they were lucky. That is a more honest account of a technology transition than the field usually gives itself.   Three things from the clip worth your time.   OCT has its own Moore's law. Commercial scan speed doubles roughly every 2.7 years, and every jump in speed opens something new. Ultra-widefield imaging of almost the whole retina, which his group is applying to retinopathy of prematurity, capturing a neonate's full retina in about twenty seconds in infrared light that does not disturb the baby. OCT angiography down to the capillary, resolving four separate vascular plexuses inside a few hundred microns of tissue. Optoretinography, which detects photoreceptors lengthening by nanometres when they capture a photon, so you can map function and not only structure.  And on what limits the next step, his answer was speed, bounded by how much light you can safely put on a retina. AI acceleration is the open avenue. FDA clearance is what slows it down.   There is also a short exchange near the end I keep coming back to. Asked whether a portable system could catch sepsis in intensive care, Huang said it is technically very feasible, and that the real barriers are regulatory approval and the fact that intensive care doctors are not trained on OCT. In his words, it is alien technology to them. The instrument is ready before the clinic is.   We do not often get to hear how a technology actually crossed over, from the person who was there. Fifteen minutes from our two-hour Online Industry Meeting on photonics in ophthalmology and vision care.

THE SMALLEST SPECTROMETER IN THE NETWORK COMES FROM MILAN. The Optica events travel season restarts next week. My first stop is Milan, Italy visiting Optica corporate members. Here is a preview of one of them.   I sat down with Douglas Aguiar, CEO and co-founder of PhotonPath.   Almost every AI infrastructure conversation this year has been about scale-up and scale-out. PhotonPath went after scale-across, and did it on purpose. That is where the network stops pretending to be digital. Fibre-dependent loss, different gains from different amplifiers, spectral shapes that have to be held in place. Douglas put it plainly: they picked the part of the market where the analog problems are hardest, because that is the part they know how to handle.   Their answer is the nanoOCM, an optical channel monitor small enough to plug into a switch or a router. 500 millisecond scan time. Minus 35 dBm sensitivity. Douglas says it is the first pluggable OCM on the market, and that the pluggability, not the physics, is what customers react to first. No integration project. You plug it in and you can see your DWDM channels.   The platform choice is the interesting part. Not standard silicon photonics. Silicon oxynitride. His argument is about power. Parallel links between AI clusters need optical power that a silicon waveguide will not take at 23 to 25 dBm without nonlinearities showing up. Silicon oxynitride, in his words, is the sweet spot between a compact device and one that tolerates high output power.   It is also built for flex grid. With 800G deployed, 1.6T arriving and 3.2T ahead, nobody knows today how wide their channels will need to be tomorrow. So the customer sets the channel plan and picks which channels to watch.   Then the unglamorous part, which is where European component companies live or die. PhotonPath ships bare chips on carrier to customers with their own assembly capability, and finished modules to those without. Douglas describes the company as an orchestration layer: their chip designs, other people's fabs, assembly and test, one qualified product at the end. The nanoOCM passed Telcordia GR-468, GR-63 and GR-78 last September. The company closed a 5.1 million euro Series A in June 2025, and Douglas told me a Series B opens in a few months.   My read is that this is what a European photonics company looks like when it grows up. Founded in 2019 as a 義大利米蘭理工大學 spin-off, in a city whose optical networking culture runs back to Pirelli Labs, now selling a certified product into telecom and AI data centre networks instead of a promising demo.   Milan was building optical networks twenty years ago. It still is. That step, from spin-off to qualified supplier, is the one our community needs to hear more often.

AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Yunnan Chihong Zinc&Germanium Co., Ltd. scaling 6 inch substrates, San'An Optoelectronics Co., Ltd. running substrate to chip in a single house. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. WHEN THE DRONE TETHER IS MADE OF GLASS  I listened to a 英國廣播公司 Radio 4 documentary this week called Britain's Robot Army. One passing detail stopped me, and I think it belongs to our industry rather than to the defence press.  The drones reshaping the front line in Ukraine are increasingly guided by a bare optical fibre paying out from a spool bolted to the airframe. No radio link, so nothing to jam. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

They are H4RG-10 mercury cadmium telluride sensor chip assemblies with Teledyne Space Imaging Sensors. Teledyne delivered 28 flight-grade units against a requirement of 24, and reported that all of them beat specification on quantum efficiency, noise and image persistence.  Read that yield number again. Filling 24 slots with 28 qualified parts is a manufacturing statement, not just a physics one.  The second instrument is the one our community should study. Roman's Coronagraph carries two deformable mirrors about 5 cm across, each with more than 1600 actuators, from Xinetics, Inc. at Northrop Grumman. NASA says the surfaces are commanded to 62 picometers. Behind the masks sit filters, Wollaston prisms for polarimetry, prisms for spectroscopy, and an electron-multiplying CCD counting single photons at minus 90 C, with Teledyne e2vv and Nüvü Caméras Inc. named on the detector and camera side.  The physics is simple to state. You cannot block a star's glare with a mask alone, because diffraction and small optical imperfections scatter light back into the image. So you measure that scattered light and reshape the mirror to cancel it, continuously. One detail got lost. Roman's 2.4 metre primary was donated by the National Reconnaissance Office from a cancelled programme. It was not a drop-in. Julie McEnery, Roman's senior project scientist, has said the team had to refigure the optical prescription and change the structure to operate at lower temperatures. Free hardware is not free optics.  My take is that the control loop, not the telescope, is the transferable asset. Picometer-class wavefront sensing and control is the same engineering problem as semiconductor metrology, high numerical aperture lithography optics, free space optical links and laser communication terminals. Space qualified it. The ground market will use it. One honest caveat. The Coronagraph flies as a technology demonstration, and it was reclassified as one during development to control cost. It does not prove that Earth-sized planets can be imaged, and it should not be described that way.  What I read from this launch is not a discovery. It is a supply chain. Large format infrared arrays at yield, photon counting detectors and precision actuated optics are all now flight proven, built by companies Optica members work with every day.  The astronomy arrives in 2027. The industrial capability is already here!

AN AI AGENT JUST LEARNED TO FIX A LASER LOCK. WHY THIS IS A PHOTONICS STORY, NOT THE MICROSCOPES. Anthropic opened a research preview last week of the Model Hardware Standard, MHS. It gives an AI agent one common way to discover and operate physical instruments. Each device gets a driver with read and write primitives, plus plain language tags describing what it does and the safety limits it must not cross.   The coverage went to pipetting robots and microscopes. The result our industry should read came from QuEra Computing Inc..   QuEra builds neutral-atom quantum computers that stop when a laser loses lock. Four specialists had already spent two to three weeks writing a recovery script by hand. Working through MHS, Claude ran its own experiments on a dedicated laser testbed inside engineer-set limits, then wrote conventional software the engineers could inspect and sign off.   Relock went from 150 seconds at 58 percent success to 6 seconds at 96 percent. In a blind test it recovered the lock in 695 of 700 trials across seven fault types, with no false reports of success. Human specialists needed 5 to 10 minutes.   So is this only useful for prototyping?   A 300mm fab does not have the problem MHS solves. Production equipment has spoken SECS/GEM since the 1980s and EDA since the 2000s. That layer is settled and governed.   Photonics hurts downstream of the fab, namely n test, alignment and packaging. High mix, multi-vendor, script-driven. Tunable lasers, power meters, polarisation controllers, piezo stages and thermal chucks from six suppliers, glued together with custom code that gets rewritten for every product. 美國卡內基美隆大學 went from raw equipment to a finished measurement curve in eight hours using MHS, against several weeks for conventional vendor setup. That is our problem, not the fab's.   For a scaler, the value is the artefact, not the agent. Claude never sat in QuEra's control loop. It developed the routine and handed over deterministic code. Agent in process development, script in production. That is a shape quality and audit can live with.   What it does not fix: an agent will not make a piezo stage settle faster. Alignment time per die is mechanics and physics.   Now look at who is building MHS support. Amazon Web Services (AWS), Danaher, Doosan Robotics, QIAGEN, Tecan, Universal Robots, Hugging FaceFace, Raspberry Pi Foundation. Life sciences and robotics company. Not one photonics test or alignment vendor. That is strange. Why not?    Our benches are already full of programmable instruments. SCPI and VISA have been standard for decades. An MHS driver for a tunable laser or an alignment stage is a smaller job than for most biology hardware, and the payoff is larger because our mix is worse.   My read is that whoever in photonics writes the first good drivers will shape what the rest of us inherit. Video below from Anthropic. https://lnkd.in/ebfsTqUC

Xanadu, Project OPTIMISM LANDS AND ITS IMPACT ON THE GLOBAL QUANTUM SUPPLY CHAIN  In June, at the Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, Xanadu's Chief Operating Officer told the room the company was setting up a 160,000 square foot facility in Toronto to bring heterogeneous integration in-house. On Thursday, August 27th, they got a loan, not a grant, with repayments set as a percentage of future revenue.   Rafal Janik was keynoting our photonic quantum computing session, the first time Xanadu had spoken at an Optica industry event. Asked from the floor in the clip below about supply chain concentration in thin film lithium niobate, he gave an answer that reads differently now:   "Global supply chains are absolutely an issue. The really good thing is that quantum has been identified as a strategic priority for pretty much every single government in the world, so everybody's trying to onshore a lot of these materials now."   Thursday was that sentence turning into a building.   The facility is called Inception. A former Campbell's soup plant in Etobicoke, anchoring a CAD 893 million project, 275 technical jobs. Cleanrooms for heterogeneous integration, round the clock wafer level test, a systems integration centre where modules are verified before they go into racks.   That is a packaging and assembly plant. The quantum computer is the customer.   Janik was explicit in Glasgow about why it has to exist. Xanadu runs three material stacks, silicon nitride, thin film lithium niobate and III-V, and building them separately is no longer sufficient. They have to be integrated. Heterogeneous integration is the bottleneck, and it is a packaging problem before it is a physics problem.   Now look at who supplies the tools. ASMPT Ltd, Bluefors, DISCO, EV Group, ficonTECTEC and 旺矽科技股份有限公司. Singapore, Finland, Japan, Austria, Germany, Taiwan. Three of the six are European. Canada is buying supply chain sovereignty, and a large part of that supply chain is European.   I do not say that as criticism. It is the honest shape of our industry. Nobody sets up a photonic packaging line alone, because the equipment base is thin and spread across firms that have each spent decades becoming very good at one step.   The caveat matters. A packaging plant does not solve fault tolerance. Heterogeneous integration at production yield is unproven at this scale, and Inception is announced rather than running. My read is that the durable asset is the line itself. If photonic fault tolerance takes longer than its advocates expect, Canada still owns a general-purpose photonic integration capability. Those are scarce, and they are useful to AI hardware, telecom and sensing, whatever happens to qubits.   For European photonics companies the lesson is not to envy the cheque. When a government funds quantum manufacturing, a large share of it lands on equipment vendors. Europe is strong there. That is a position to defend deliberately, not one to assume will hold.

David Huang's presentation (15 min) from the Optica OIM on Photonics in Ophthalmology & Vision Care August 25th is worth a wider audience. OCT did not win because it was the best physics. It won because someone could bill for it.   David Huang co-invented optical coherence tomography, and in this clip he tells the origin story himself. It began as close to a pure physics experiment, using light to measure time of flight and see below a surface, in Professor Fujimoto's lab at MIT while he was a PhD student.   Then the dates.   First publication, 1991. First patent, 1994. First FDA cleared system, from Humphrey Zeiss, 1996. First CPT code, meaning a clinician could finally charge for the scan, 1997.   Six years from paper to reimbursement.   Adoption followed the billing code. Once the scan could be paid for, the revenue funded better instruments, which widened the clinical case, which justified better reimbursement. OCT did not even have that code to itself. It shared 92135 with retinal thickness analysers, slit scan tomography and scanning laser polarimetry, and took the market on depth resolution.   Huang is unusually direct about the rest of it. Regulatory steps were easier then, the founders did everything right, and they were lucky. That is a more honest account of a technology transition than the field usually gives itself.   Three things from the clip worth your time.   OCT has its own Moore's law. Commercial scan speed doubles roughly every 2.7 years, and every jump in speed opens something new. Ultra-widefield imaging of almost the whole retina, which his group is applying to retinopathy of prematurity, capturing a neonate's full retina in about twenty seconds in infrared light that does not disturb the baby. OCT angiography down to the capillary, resolving four separate vascular plexuses inside a few hundred microns of tissue. Optoretinography, which detects photoreceptors lengthening by nanometres when they capture a photon, so you can map function and not only structure.  And on what limits the next step, his answer was speed, bounded by how much light you can safely put on a retina. AI acceleration is the open avenue. FDA clearance is what slows it down.   There is also a short exchange near the end I keep coming back to. Asked whether a portable system could catch sepsis in intensive care, Huang said it is technically very feasible, and that the real barriers are regulatory approval and the fact that intensive care doctors are not trained on OCT. In his words, it is alien technology to them. The instrument is ready before the clinic is.   We do not often get to hear how a technology actually crossed over, from the person who was there. Fifteen minutes from our two-hour Online Industry Meeting on photonics in ophthalmology and vision care.

THE SMALLEST SPECTROMETER IN THE NETWORK COMES FROM MILAN. The Optica events travel season restarts next week. My first stop is Milan, Italy visiting Optica corporate members. Here is a preview of one of them.   I sat down with Douglas Aguiar, CEO and co-founder of PhotonPath.   Almost every AI infrastructure conversation this year has been about scale-up and scale-out. PhotonPath went after scale-across, and did it on purpose. That is where the network stops pretending to be digital. Fibre-dependent loss, different gains from different amplifiers, spectral shapes that have to be held in place. Douglas put it plainly: they picked the part of the market where the analog problems are hardest, because that is the part they know how to handle.   Their answer is the nanoOCM, an optical channel monitor small enough to plug into a switch or a router. 500 millisecond scan time. Minus 35 dBm sensitivity. Douglas says it is the first pluggable OCM on the market, and that the pluggability, not the physics, is what customers react to first. No integration project. You plug it in and you can see your DWDM channels.   The platform choice is the interesting part. Not standard silicon photonics. Silicon oxynitride. His argument is about power. Parallel links between AI clusters need optical power that a silicon waveguide will not take at 23 to 25 dBm without nonlinearities showing up. Silicon oxynitride, in his words, is the sweet spot between a compact device and one that tolerates high output power.   It is also built for flex grid. With 800G deployed, 1.6T arriving and 3.2T ahead, nobody knows today how wide their channels will need to be tomorrow. So the customer sets the channel plan and picks which channels to watch.   Then the unglamorous part, which is where European component companies live or die. PhotonPath ships bare chips on carrier to customers with their own assembly capability, and finished modules to those without. Douglas describes the company as an orchestration layer: their chip designs, other people's fabs, assembly and test, one qualified product at the end. The nanoOCM passed Telcordia GR-468, GR-63 and GR-78 last September. The company closed a 5.1 million euro Series A in June 2025, and Douglas told me a Series B opens in a few months.   My read is that this is what a European photonics company looks like when it grows up. Founded in 2019 as a 義大利米蘭理工大學 spin-off, in a city whose optical networking culture runs back to Pirelli Labs, now selling a certified product into telecom and AI data centre networks instead of a promising demo.   Milan was building optical networks twenty years ago. It still is. That step, from spin-off to qualified supplier, is the one our community needs to hear more often.

AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align.  This ties in perfectly with the work being done by QURECA, which was recently highlighted at the Quantum ARC event in Glasgow.
