THIS CONFERENCE WORKS BECAUSE PEOPLE SAY WHAT THEY NEED Most industry events are showcases. Ours is built the other way round. Every speaker at the recent Optica Quantum Industry Summit gets the same two questions: what can you do for others, and what can others do for you. The enabling technologies session opened with the chair telling the room that end users and integrators should say what they actually need, not what they already sell.  Tim Day, Chairman and Chief Executive of Monarch Quantum, took fifteen minutes and used almost none of it on physics.  Monarch is six months old. The playbook is not. Day has spent three decades moving photonics out of the laboratory and into production. He co-founded New Focus, which built photonics subsystems for telecom hardware, took it public and merged it with a British multinational. He then did the same in aerospace and defence, a business he says is close to shipping a billion dollars of photonic subsystems and turns over 150 to 200 million a year. Monarch was spun out of that work to serve quantum. Around 120 engineers and scientists, in San Diego.  His opening claim is the one worth arguing about. In the quantum systems he works on, photonics is 40 to 65 per cent of the bill of materials.  Then he did the arithmetic. A 10,000-qubit machine can involve more than 100,000 optical components. Give every component a 10,000-hour lifetime, put them in series, and the system lasts six minutes! That is the case against carrying laboratory instruments into products. Not that they perform badly. They perform beautifully. They cannot be manufactured and they cannot stay up.  Monarch’s answer is co-packaged optics for quantum, re-engineered from the bond joint up and assembled robotically. He was careful about PICs. They will matter, but they do not yet cover UV to near infrared at the losses quantum needs, so micro-optic packaging does the work today.  The useful part was what he found underneath everyone’s different architecture. About a dozen recurring functions. Narrow linewidth lasers in several colours, electro-optic and acousto-optic modulation, amplitude control, fibre launch, amplify and split, replicating one frequency across six to twelve channels. Standardise those and you have a platform, built in automated work cells, at red, green, blue and near infrared instead of telecom wavelengths. He is deliberately agnostic. Atom, ion or photon based, he does not claim to know which wins, only that quantum does.  He is building a factory with more than 25 production work cells. Monarch holds more than 60 million dollars in customer contracts and raised 55 million this year. His answer to the Optica question was a request, not a pitch. Tell him what subsystems you need and he will tell you whether it is already on the platform.  That is the conversation our industry is short of.

WHY IonQ TOOK THE OPTICS OUT OF ITS MOST IMPORTANT OPERATION Mihir Bhaskar opened his keynote at the recent Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow with a line that should stop a photonics audience. IonQ has moved the two-qubit gate, the hardest operation in a trapped ion computer, off the lasers and onto an RF line in the chip. His reasoning was blunt.   Optics are harder to engineer, scale and integrate than electronics.  Nine things worth taking from his excellent talk- worth watching in full on Youtube. https://lnkd.in/eehmD3ni  IonQ has changed shape. Eighteen months ago it was a quantum computing company. It is now four lines: computing, networking, security and sensing. watch their 2026 Investor event on September 8th. https://lnkd.in/e86pVFbh The most critical operation is electronic now. Control is integrated into the trap chip, built on more than a decade of work in Oxford. He quotes about 99.99 per cent two qubit gate fidelity, and a trap that scales as a 2D grid using semiconductor fabrication.  Photonics moved rather than left. Cooling and readout stay optical and are being integrated into zones on the trap. Getting to 10,000 qubits is largely a photonic integration problem.  The interconnect problem is a loss problem with a number on it. About 20 dB to get a photon from an ion into single mode fibre, the same as 100 km of SMF-28. Paid at both ends, that is one success in 10,000 attempts.  Quantum memory is the fix, and the processor does not change. A memory between two processors lets the link run asynchronously. His figures: around 99 per cent storage fidelity, about 3 dB heralding loss, over 100 MHz bandwidth.  Diamond is becoming manufacturable. Thin film diamond, with Element Six in the UK. His comparison: diamond today looks like lithium niobate ten years ago.  A packaging spec you can hold a supplier to. Below 0.2 dB waveguide to fibre at visible wavelengths, in diamond, silicon nitride, silicon, lithium niobate and III-Vs. Not yet space qualified.  The economics work in the data centre first. Interconnect is 20 to 40 per cent of the cost of an NVIDIA cluster, so a quantum interconnect can be expensive and still be viable. A dated roadmap. 2026, the network runs faster than the processor. 2027, multiple channels and compatibility with other platforms. 2028, logical qubits moving between processors.  The rest is in the full video. https://lnkd.in/eehmD3ni The atomic clocks, the timing argument behind a thousand times better positioning, why IonQ bought a fab, and Chris Myatt of QPICs asking the question everyone wanted asked - about a captive foundry.

THE TELESCOPE IS THE HEADLINE. BUT THE INSTRUMENT IS PHOTONICS. NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Sunday morning (August 30th 2026) from Kennedy Space Center. It is now on a roughly 100 day cruise to L2, with first images expected in early 2027. The NASA coverage below is all about dark energy and exoplanets. But lets look at what is inside the spacecraft to make it all possible.  Roman's Wide Field Instrument is a 300-megapixel infrared camera made from 18 arrays, each 4096 by 4096 pixels on a 10 micron pitch. They are H4RG-10 mercury cadmium telluride sensor chip assemblies with Teledyne Space Imaging Sensors. Teledyne delivered 28 flight-grade units against a requirement of 24, and reported that all of them beat specification on quantum efficiency, noise and image persistence.  Read that yield number again. Filling 24 slots with 28 qualified parts is a manufacturing statement, not just a physics one.  The second instrument is the one our community should study. Roman's Coronagraph carries two deformable mirrors about 5 cm across, each with more than 1600 actuators, from Xinetics, Inc. at Northrop Grumman. NASA says the surfaces are commanded to 62 picometers. Behind the masks sit filters, Wollaston prisms for polarimetry, prisms for spectroscopy, and an electron-multiplying CCD counting single photons at minus 90 C, with Teledyne e2vv and Nüvü Caméras Inc. named on the detector and camera side.  The physics is simple to state. You cannot block a star's glare with a mask alone, because diffraction and small optical imperfections scatter light back into the image. So you measure that scattered light and reshape the mirror to cancel it, continuously. One detail got lost. Roman's 2.4 metre primary was donated by the National Reconnaissance Office from a cancelled programme. It was not a drop-in. Julie McEnery, Roman's senior project scientist, has said the team had to refigure the optical prescription and change the structure to operate at lower temperatures. Free hardware is not free optics.  My take is that the control loop, not the telescope, is the transferable asset. Picometer-class wavefront sensing and control is the same engineering problem as semiconductor metrology, high numerical aperture lithography optics, free space optical links and laser communication terminals. Space qualified it. The ground market will use it. One honest caveat. The Coronagraph flies as a technology demonstration, and it was reclassified as one during development to control cost. It does not prove that Earth-sized planets can be imaged, and it should not be described that way.  What I read from this launch is not a discovery. It is a supply chain. Large format infrared arrays at yield, photon counting detectors and precision actuated optics are all now flight proven, built by companies Optica members work with every day.  The astronomy arrives in 2027. The industrial capability is already here!

AN AI AGENT JUST LEARNED TO FIX A LASER LOCK. WHY THIS IS A PHOTONICS STORY, NOT THE MICROSCOPES. Anthropic opened a research preview last week of the Model Hardware Standard, MHS. It gives an AI agent one common way to discover and operate physical instruments. Each device gets a driver with read and write primitives, plus plain language tags describing what it does and the safety limits it must not cross.   The coverage went to pipetting robots and microscopes. The result our industry should read came from QuEra Computing Inc..   QuEra builds neutral-atom quantum computers that stop when a laser loses lock. Four specialists had already spent two to three weeks writing a recovery script by hand. Working through MHS, Claude ran its own experiments on a dedicated laser testbed inside engineer-set limits, then wrote conventional software the engineers could inspect and sign off.   Relock went from 150 seconds at 58 percent success to 6 seconds at 96 percent. In a blind test it recovered the lock in 695 of 700 trials across seven fault types, with no false reports of success. Human specialists needed 5 to 10 minutes.   So is this only useful for prototyping?   A 300mm fab does not have the problem MHS solves. Production equipment has spoken SECS/GEM since the 1980s and EDA since the 2000s. That layer is settled and governed.   Photonics hurts downstream of the fab, namely n test, alignment and packaging. High mix, multi-vendor, script-driven. Tunable lasers, power meters, polarisation controllers, piezo stages and thermal chucks from six suppliers, glued together with custom code that gets rewritten for every product. 美國卡內基美隆大學 went from raw equipment to a finished measurement curve in eight hours using MHS, against several weeks for conventional vendor setup. That is our problem, not the fab's.   For a scaler, the value is the artefact, not the agent. Claude never sat in QuEra's control loop. It developed the routine and handed over deterministic code. Agent in process development, script in production. That is a shape quality and audit can live with.   What it does not fix: an agent will not make a piezo stage settle faster. Alignment time per die is mechanics and physics.   Now look at who is building MHS support. Amazon Web Services (AWS), Danaher, Doosan Robotics, QIAGEN, Tecan, Universal Robots, Hugging FaceFace, Raspberry Pi Foundation. Life sciences and robotics company. Not one photonics test or alignment vendor. That is strange. Why not?    Our benches are already full of programmable instruments. SCPI and VISA have been standard for decades. An MHS driver for a tunable laser or an alignment stage is a smaller job than for most biology hardware, and the payoff is larger because our mix is worse.   My read is that whoever in photonics writes the first good drivers will shape what the rest of us inherit. Video below from Anthropic. https://lnkd.in/ebfsTqUC

Xanadu, Project OPTIMISM LANDS AND ITS IMPACT ON THE GLOBAL QUANTUM SUPPLY CHAIN  In June, at the Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, Xanadu's Chief Operating Officer told the room the company was setting up a 160,000 square foot facility in Toronto to bring heterogeneous integration in-house. On Thursday, August 27th, they got a loan, not a grant, with repayments set as a percentage of future revenue.   Rafal Janik was keynoting our photonic quantum computing session, the first time Xanadu had spoken at an Optica industry event. Asked from the floor in the clip below about supply chain concentration in thin film lithium niobate, he gave an answer that reads differently now:   "Global supply chains are absolutely an issue. The really good thing is that quantum has been identified as a strategic priority for pretty much every single government in the world, so everybody's trying to onshore a lot of these materials now."   Thursday was that sentence turning into a building.   The facility is called Inception. A former Campbell's soup plant in Etobicoke, anchoring a CAD 893 million project, 275 technical jobs. Cleanrooms for heterogeneous integration, round the clock wafer level test, a systems integration centre where modules are verified before they go into racks.   That is a packaging and assembly plant. The quantum computer is the customer.   Janik was explicit in Glasgow about why it has to exist. Xanadu runs three material stacks, silicon nitride, thin film lithium niobate and III-V, and building them separately is no longer sufficient. They have to be integrated. Heterogeneous integration is the bottleneck, and it is a packaging problem before it is a physics problem.   Now look at who supplies the tools. ASMPT Ltd, Bluefors, DISCO, EV Group, ficonTECTEC and 旺矽科技股份有限公司. Singapore, Finland, Japan, Austria, Germany, Taiwan. Three of the six are European. Canada is buying supply chain sovereignty, and a large part of that supply chain is European.   I do not say that as criticism. It is the honest shape of our industry. Nobody sets up a photonic packaging line alone, because the equipment base is thin and spread across firms that have each spent decades becoming very good at one step.   The caveat matters. A packaging plant does not solve fault tolerance. Heterogeneous integration at production yield is unproven at this scale, and Inception is announced rather than running. My read is that the durable asset is the line itself. If photonic fault tolerance takes longer than its advocates expect, Canada still owns a general-purpose photonic integration capability. Those are scarce, and they are useful to AI hardware, telecom and sensing, whatever happens to qubits.   For European photonics companies the lesson is not to envy the cheque. When a government funds quantum manufacturing, a large share of it lands on equipment vendors. Europe is strong there. That is a position to defend deliberately, not one to assume will hold.

David Huang's presentation (15 min) from the Optica OIM on Photonics in Ophthalmology & Vision Care August 25th is worth a wider audience. OCT did not win because it was the best physics. It won because someone could bill for it.   David Huang co-invented optical coherence tomography, and in this clip he tells the origin story himself. It began as close to a pure physics experiment, using light to measure time of flight and see below a surface, in Professor Fujimoto's lab at MIT while he was a PhD student.   Then the dates.   First publication, 1991. First patent, 1994. First FDA cleared system, from Humphrey Zeiss, 1996. First CPT code, meaning a clinician could finally charge for the scan, 1997.   Six years from paper to reimbursement.   Adoption followed the billing code. Once the scan could be paid for, the revenue funded better instruments, which widened the clinical case, which justified better reimbursement. OCT did not even have that code to itself. It shared 92135 with retinal thickness analysers, slit scan tomography and scanning laser polarimetry, and took the market on depth resolution.   Huang is unusually direct about the rest of it. Regulatory steps were easier then, the founders did everything right, and they were lucky. That is a more honest account of a technology transition than the field usually gives itself.   Three things from the clip worth your time.   OCT has its own Moore's law. Commercial scan speed doubles roughly every 2.7 years, and every jump in speed opens something new. Ultra-widefield imaging of almost the whole retina, which his group is applying to retinopathy of prematurity, capturing a neonate's full retina in about twenty seconds in infrared light that does not disturb the baby. OCT angiography down to the capillary, resolving four separate vascular plexuses inside a few hundred microns of tissue. Optoretinography, which detects photoreceptors lengthening by nanometres when they capture a photon, so you can map function and not only structure.  And on what limits the next step, his answer was speed, bounded by how much light you can safely put on a retina. AI acceleration is the open avenue. FDA clearance is what slows it down.   There is also a short exchange near the end I keep coming back to. Asked whether a portable system could catch sepsis in intensive care, Huang said it is technically very feasible, and that the real barriers are regulatory approval and the fact that intensive care doctors are not trained on OCT. In his words, it is alien technology to them. The instrument is ready before the clinic is.   We do not often get to hear how a technology actually crossed over, from the person who was there. Fifteen minutes from our two-hour Online Industry Meeting on photonics in ophthalmology and vision care.

THE SMALLEST SPECTROMETER IN THE NETWORK COMES FROM MILAN. The Optica events travel season restarts next week. My first stop is Milan, Italy visiting Optica corporate members. Here is a preview of one of them.   I sat down with Douglas Aguiar, CEO and co-founder of PhotonPath.   Almost every AI infrastructure conversation this year has been about scale-up and scale-out. PhotonPath went after scale-across, and did it on purpose. That is where the network stops pretending to be digital. Fibre-dependent loss, different gains from different amplifiers, spectral shapes that have to be held in place. Douglas put it plainly: they picked the part of the market where the analog problems are hardest, because that is the part they know how to handle.   Their answer is the nanoOCM, an optical channel monitor small enough to plug into a switch or a router. 500 millisecond scan time. Minus 35 dBm sensitivity. Douglas says it is the first pluggable OCM on the market, and that the pluggability, not the physics, is what customers react to first. No integration project. You plug it in and you can see your DWDM channels.   The platform choice is the interesting part. Not standard silicon photonics. Silicon oxynitride. His argument is about power. Parallel links between AI clusters need optical power that a silicon waveguide will not take at 23 to 25 dBm without nonlinearities showing up. Silicon oxynitride, in his words, is the sweet spot between a compact device and one that tolerates high output power.   It is also built for flex grid. With 800G deployed, 1.6T arriving and 3.2T ahead, nobody knows today how wide their channels will need to be tomorrow. So the customer sets the channel plan and picks which channels to watch.   Then the unglamorous part, which is where European component companies live or die. PhotonPath ships bare chips on carrier to customers with their own assembly capability, and finished modules to those without. Douglas describes the company as an orchestration layer: their chip designs, other people's fabs, assembly and test, one qualified product at the end. The nanoOCM passed Telcordia GR-468, GR-63 and GR-78 last September. The company closed a 5.1 million euro Series A in June 2025, and Douglas told me a Series B opens in a few months.   My read is that this is what a European photonics company looks like when it grows up. Founded in 2019 as a 義大利米蘭理工大學 spin-off, in a city whose optical networking culture runs back to Pirelli Labs, now selling a certified product into telecom and AI data centre networks instead of a promising demo.   Milan was building optical networks twenty years ago. It still is. That step, from spin-off to qualified supplier, is the one our community needs to hear more often.

AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Yunnan Chihong Zinc&Germanium Co., Ltd. scaling 6 inch substrates, San'An Optoelectronics Co., Ltd. running substrate to chip in a single house. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. WHEN THE DRONE TETHER IS MADE OF GLASS  I listened to a 英國廣播公司 Radio 4 documentary this week called Britain's Robot Army. One passing detail stopped me, and I think it belongs to our industry rather than to the defence press.  The drones reshaping the front line in Ukraine are increasingly guided by a bare optical fibre paying out from a spool bolted to the airframe. No radio link, so nothing to jam. Nobody said who makes that fibre. So we went and found out.  Three things worth your attention.  It is not a bespoke defence product. It is ITU-T G.657.A2 bend-insensitive single-mode fibre, the same category developed for tight-radius routing in fibre-to-the-home. 1310 and 1550 nm, 250 micron coating, dynamic bend radius down to about 7.5 mm. The property that lets you turn a corner in an apartment block is the property that lets a drone unspool 30 km at speed without macrobend loss.  Fibre-guided drones and AI data centres are now bidding for the same product. A commodity telecom fibre has acquired a second, price-inelastic customer base, and our industry did not plan for that.  The specialist value has moved from the glass to the spool. Nobody draws fibre for drones. What matters is winding geometry, packing process, tension control and payout mechanics, because failures in flight are mechanical rather than optical. The firms doing that work well are small, European and American, and most of them are not yet part of our community. I spent a day in  #Enschede, The Netherlands with Tim Tiek, CEO of Brilliance RGB, witnessing a small team turn silicon nitride photonic integrated circuits into a full RGB light engine, small enough for AR glasses and thin enough for a car dashboard. PICs have lived mainly in datacom and telecom for two decades. Brilliance RGB, founded about three years ago, is pushing the same platform into a market with far higher volume: visible light for AR/VR eyewear, automotive displays, and industrial sensing. The chip integrates lasers, waveguides, and sensors onto a single wafer-scale silicon nitride platform, replacing the lenses, prisms, and discrete lasers that make traditional RGB projectors (including IMAX) bulky and expensive.  Why silicon nitride specifically? It couples laser light into waveguides with very high efficiency, which matters most for eyewear: a glasses form factor with a battery that has to last a full day of projection lives or dies on power efficiency. Tim's case for laser displays over micro-LED comes down to full colour, wide field of view, and outdoor brightness, though he's clear micro-LED still wins for simple monochrome use cases like sport glasses.  The automotive angle is just as concrete. Today's heads-up displays run on LCOS panels behind the steering wheel, bulky and lossy by design. Brilliance's approach could shrink that by a factor of ten while cutting cooling overhead, and the same chip architecture could support ground projection as self-driving cars start signalling turns and warnings to pedestrians. Tim's team is already in conversations with Tier 1 suppliers and OEMs on that.  Credibility is building fast for a three-year-old company. Google's Bernard Kress, speaking at the recent Optica summit at 康寧公司, has publicly called PICs a promising technology for next-gen AR/VR goggles, and Brilliance RGB is active in the growing laser-display ecosystem, alongside more than 40 companies now working on laser projection as a category. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

Greater Glasgow was recently ranked the fifth most important quantum cluster in the world, and first globally for its role as a sector hub. That’s an incredible achievement for the UK, and a massive nod to Scotland's deep-tech ecosystem.  This week I’ve been following discussions at Optica's Quantum 2.0 Conference in Glasgow (15–18 June) where one of the themes has been the race to translate raw R&D into practical, commercial applications.  Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica, captured the challenge. He pointed out that quantum is currently moving at two separate speeds: academic research (measured in qubits) and industry reality (focused on scalable products). At the moment, they’re not aligned. While the science is forging ahead, the market is lagging in building the next-generation hardware needed to protect our critical infrastructure.  The timeline is tight. According to some predictions, quantum hardware capable of cracking current security algorithms could exist within three years. Andrew Shields of Toshiba Europe UK thought a ten-year horizon was more realistic, but there’s great urgency nonetheless. Alongside resilient hardware, we also need new data protocols and certification standards.  It was very positive to hear about the local expertise that’s helping to address this challenge. Scottish space company Craft Prospect is already working on using satellites to facilitate Quantum Key Distribution from space – a vital step in scaling these networks from regional to global models.  For me, the key message was Jose’s rallying cry at the end of his opening presentation: ‘Connect the bench to the market’. His advice for closing the divide was direct:  ⚛️ To the researchers: Bring the hard problems and the honest data – not the press release. 🏢 To industry: Bring the real-world use cases, the capital, and the procurement appetite to make deployment a reality.  In a sector changing this quickly, clear communication is going to play a key role. Alongside the researchers and companies developing the tech, we need to educate the wider community about what quantum will offer – the great benefits, but also the threats to our critical infrastructure and daily lives if research and industry don’t align.  This ties in perfectly with the work being done by QURECA, which was recently highlighted at the Quantum ARC event in Glasgow. That marked the launch of a new report titled ‘Inside Scotland’s Quantum Ecosystem’ – yet another reminder of the country’s key role in the quantum race.

WHAT DID QUIX JUST MAKE OBSOLETE? EVERY PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER THAT CAME BEFORE IT. That was the claim from Jelmer Renema, co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuiX Quantum, at last week's Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, collocated this year with Quantum 2.0. On the exhibition floor, he announced Carina, which QuiX is calling the first universal photonic quantum computer deployed to a customer site.  Universal is the operative word. It means the machine can execute any quantum algorithm, including the famous ones like Shor's and Grover's that require arbitrary quantum computation rather than a narrow set of operations tailored to the hardware. Until now, most of the field has been building algorithms to fit the computer. QuiX is arguing the order should be reversed.  The technology that makes this possible, according to Renema, is feed-forward. A photonic computer works by sending photons through an optical system. If you can switch that optical system in real time based on what some of the photons are doing, you can steer it toward arbitrary quantum computations. Doing that at the speed of light demands a tight combination of fast electronics, high-quality detectors, precise optics, and nonlinear optics, all integrated into a single package. Bringing those components together in a deployed device is what QuiX says makes prior delivered systems obsolete.  Carina is NOT a lab demonstration. Renema said it is in production, commercially available, and purchasable today, with cloud access already live through QuiX's website. The design choices are aimed squarely at the AI data center buildout: room temperature operation, modular architecture, and scaling through fiber connections, which positions photonic quantum hardware to ride the same infrastructure wave that is already pulling photonics into data centers.  On scaling, Renema was direct about the open problems the Summit kept returning to: losses in fiber to chip coupling and modulator efficiency. His case for optimism is that the hardware requirements can be relaxed through software. He pointed to the long-run reduction in qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm, and to a photonics-tailored error correction strategy QuiX says outperforms conventional quantum error correction by a factor of four, lowering the cost of the machine.  The roadmap from here is utility scale: large systems of interlinked, fiber-coupled optical racks on a data center floor, stabilized and controlled by a classical computer alongside them, running real industry workloads. With Xanadu, PsiQuantum, IonQ and others in the room, Renema's summary of the week was blunt. The race is on, and quantum utility is now on the horizon.

In part one posted earlier today, Jan-Jurien de Rijck explained why defence packaging has to start with the environment rather than the chip. Here the conversation moves to volume, and to Europe.   The demo first. The interrogator was shaking on the table and still reading a carbon plate in real time, resolving its 3D shape as I twisted it. That is helicopter blade deformation monitoring. PhotonFirst has been building these systems for the defence and aerospace domain for around twenty years, and photonic integrated circuits are what let them ruggedise the optics.   Then the number every CTO asks about. In house, PhotonFirst can scale to around 5,000 units a year. Beyond that they transfer the technology to OSAT partners while keeping ownership of it, and set the line up as a service to the customer. That is a sensible answer to a problem a lot of European photonics companies have not yet had to solve.   Leendert-Jan Nijstad, the CEO, was direct about Europe. Two advantages, in his account. In chip-based optical systems there are still minor dependencies outside Europe, and the work to remove them is not finished. Sovereignty here is a direction of travel, not a status anyone has reached.   His ambition for the next five years: everybody talks about lab to fab, and in the optical world he wants lab to fab to flight, with high volume production stories behind it.   My read is that the constraint on photonics in European defence is neither physics nor chips. It is qualified capacity. The companies that can carry a system from design through MIL standard qualification to a repeatable line are the bottleneck, and that list is short.   This is the beginning of a series. DESIGN FOR THE ROTOR BLADE, NOT FOR THE CHIP: PHOTONFIRST GRAND TOUR PART ONE Most conversations about photonic packaging start with the chip. For defence, that is already the wrong starting point. We went to PhotonFirst in Alkmaar, The Netherlands, because at Optica we want to understand how the photonics supply chain actually looks for defence applications. European governments are raising the share of GDP they spend on defence. Our industry keeps saying photonics is strategic. I wanted to see what that means on a factory floor.   Jan-Jurien de Rijck walked me through the cleanroom, and gave me the comparison that stayed with me. A data centre against an Apache helicopter. Put a system on a rotor blade and shock, vibration and electromagnetic compatibility stop being tests you run at the end. They set the design from the first day.   The standards do the talking. DO-160 in the civil domain. MIL-STD-461 for EMC and MIL-STD-810 for shock, vibration and moisture ingress in the military domain. Those requirements flow down from system level to package level, which is the reason the package cannot be designed after the chip is finished.   One process makes it concrete. The fibre-to-chip connection has long been the weak point in these systems. PhotonFirst uses lensed fibre laser welding rather than adhesive, because glue struggles under thermal load. Fibre array welding is still in development.   And there is a product to point at rather than a capability claim. A digital sun sensor for satellite navigation, qualified to DO-160, built in the hundreds on a dedicated production line.   For twenty years we have told people to think about the package before the chip. What I heard in Alkmaar goes one step further back. Think about the environment first, then the system, then the package, then the chip.   My read is that this is the part of the supply chain Europe consistently underestimates. We argue about foundries and about chips. The step that decides whether a photonic system survives a rotor blade is packaging and qualification, and the number of European companies that can take that all the way to a qualified system is small.   Part two in the next post covers the shaker table demo, and what happens when a defence customer asks for volume. Thanks also to Emma Xu, PhD and Mirvais Yousefi for help behind the scenes. THIS CONFERENCE WORKS BECAUSE PEOPLE SAY WHAT THEY NEED Most industry events are showcases. Ours is built the other way round. Every speaker at the recent Optica Quantum Industry Summit gets the same two questions: what can you do for others, and what can others do for you. The enabling technologies session opened with the chair telling the room that end users and integrators should say what they actually need, not what they already sell.  Tim Day, Chairman and Chief Executive of Monarch Quantum, took fifteen minutes and used almost none of it on physics.  Monarch is six months old. The playbook is not. Day has spent three decades moving photonics out of the laboratory and into production. He co-founded New Focus, which built photonics subsystems for telecom hardware, took it public and merged it with a British multinational. He then did the same in aerospace and defence, a business he says is close to shipping a billion dollars of photonic subsystems and turns over 150 to 200 million a year. Monarch was spun out of that work to serve quantum. Around 120 engineers and scientists, in San Diego.  His opening claim is the one worth arguing about. In the quantum systems he works on, photonics is 40 to 65 per cent of the bill of materials.  Then he did the arithmetic. A 10,000-qubit machine can involve more than 100,000 optical components. Give every component a 10,000-hour lifetime, put them in series, and the system lasts six minutes! That is the case against carrying laboratory instruments into products. Not that they perform badly. They perform beautifully. They cannot be manufactured and they cannot stay up.  Monarch’s answer is co-packaged optics for quantum, re-engineered from the bond joint up and assembled robotically. He was careful about PICs. They will matter, but they do not yet cover UV to near infrared at the losses quantum needs, so micro-optic packaging does the work today.  The useful part was what he found underneath everyone’s different architecture. About a dozen recurring functions. Narrow linewidth lasers in several colours, electro-optic and acousto-optic modulation, amplitude control, fibre launch, amplify and split, replicating one frequency across six to twelve channels. Standardise those and you have a platform, built in automated work cells, at red, green, blue and near infrared instead of telecom wavelengths. He is deliberately agnostic. Atom, ion or photon based, he does not claim to know which wins, only that quantum does.  He is building a factory with more than 25 production work cells. Monarch holds more than 60 million dollars in customer contracts and raised 55 million this year. His answer to the Optica question was a request, not a pitch. Tell him what subsystems you need and he will tell you whether it is already on the platform.  That is the conversation our industry is short of.

IonQ has moved the two-qubit gate, the hardest operation in a trapped ion computer, off the lasers and onto an RF line in the chip. His reasoning was blunt.   Optics are harder to engineer, scale and integrate than electronics.  Nine things worth taking from his excellent talk- worth watching in full on Youtube. https://lnkd.in/eehmD3ni  IonQ has changed shape. Eighteen months ago it was a quantum computing company. It is now four lines: computing, networking, security and sensing. watch their 2026 Investor event on September 8th. https://lnkd.in/e86pVFbh The most critical operation is electronic now. Control is integrated into the trap chip, built on more than a decade of work in Oxford. He quotes about 99.99 per cent two qubit gate fidelity, and a trap that scales as a 2D grid using semiconductor fabrication.  Photonics moved rather than left. Cooling and readout stay optical and are being integrated into zones on the trap. Getting to 10,000 qubits is largely a photonic integration problem.  The interconnect problem is a loss problem with a number on it. About 20 dB to get a photon from an ion into single mode fibre, the same as 100 km of SMF-28. Paid at both ends, that is one success in 10,000 attempts.  Quantum memory is the fix, and the processor does not change. A memory between two processors lets the link run asynchronously. Interconnect is 20 to 40 per cent of the cost of an NVIDIA cluster, so a quantum interconnect can be expensive and still be viable. THE TELESCOPE IS THE HEADLINE. BUT THE INSTRUMENT IS PHOTONICS. NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Sunday morning (August 30th 2026) from Kennedy Space Center. It is now on a roughly 100 day cruise to L2, with first images expected in early 2027. The NASA coverage below is all about dark energy and exoplanets. But lets look at what is inside the spacecraft to make it all possible.  Roman's Wide Field Instrument is a 300-megapixel infrared camera made from 18 arrays, each 4096 by 4096 pixels on a 10 micron pitch. They are H4RG-10 mercury cadmium telluride sensor chip assemblies with Teledyne Space Imaging Sensors. Teledyne delivered 28 flight-grade units against a requirement of 24, and reported that all of them beat specification on quantum efficiency, noise and image persistence.  Read that yield number again. Filling 24 slots with 28 qualified parts is a manufacturing statement, not just a physics one.  The second instrument is the one our community should study. Roman's Coronagraph carries two deformable mirrors about 5 cm across, each with more than 1600 actuators, from Xinetics, Inc. at Northrop Grumman. NASA says the surfaces are commanded to 62 picometers. Behind the masks sit filters, Wollaston prisms for polarimetry, prisms for spectroscopy, and an electron-multiplying CCD counting single photons at minus 90 C, with Teledyne e2vv and Nüvü Caméras Inc. named on the detector and camera side.  The physics is simple to state. You cannot block a star's glare with a mask alone, because diffraction and small optical imperfections scatter light back into the image. So you measure that scattered light and reshape the mirror to cancel it, continuously. One detail got lost. Roman's 2.4 metre primary was donated by the National Reconnaissance Office from a cancelled programme. It was not a drop-in. Julie McEnery, Roman's senior project scientist, has said the team had to refigure the optical prescription and change the structure to operate at lower temperatures. Free hardware is not free optics.  My take is that the control loop, not the telescope, is the transferable asset. Picometer-class wavefront sensing and control is the same engineering problem as semiconductor metrology, high numerical aperture lithography optics, free space optical links and laser communication terminals. Space qualified it. The ground market will use it. One honest caveat. The Coronagraph flies as a technology demonstration, and it was reclassified as one during development to control cost. It does not prove that Earth-sized planets can be imaged, and it should not be described that way.  What I read from this launch is not a discovery. It is a supply chain. Large format infrared arrays at yield, photon counting detectors and precision actuated optics are all now flight proven, built by companies Optica members work with every day.  The astronomy arrives in 2027. The industrial capability is already here!

AN AI AGENT JUST LEARNED TO FIX A LASER LOCK. WHY THIS IS A PHOTONICS STORY, NOT THE MICROSCOPES. Anthropic opened a research preview last week of the Model Hardware Standard, MHS. It gives an AI agent one common way to discover and operate physical instruments. Each device gets a driver with read and write primitives, plus plain language tags describing what it does and the safety limits it must not cross.   The coverage went to pipetting robots and microscopes. The result our industry should read came from QuEra Computing Inc..   QuEra builds neutral-atom quantum computers that stop when a laser loses lock. Four specialists had already spent two to three weeks writing a recovery script by hand. Working through MHS, Claude ran its own experiments on a dedicated laser testbed inside engineer-set limits, then wrote conventional software the engineers could inspect and sign off.   Relock went from 150 seconds at 58 percent success to 6 seconds at 96 percent. In a blind test it recovered the lock in 695 of 700 trials across seven fault types, with no false reports of success. Human specialists needed 5 to 10 minutes.   So is this only useful for prototyping?   A 300mm fab does not have the problem MHS solves. Production equipment has spoken SECS/GEM since the 1980s and EDA since the 2000s. That layer is settled and governed.   Photonics hurts downstream of the fab, namely n test, alignment and packaging. High mix, multi-vendor, script-driven. Tunable lasers, power meters, polarisation controllers, piezo stages and thermal chucks from six suppliers, glued together with custom code that gets rewritten for every product. 美國卡內基美隆大學 went from raw equipment to a finished measurement curve in eight hours using MHS, against several weeks for conventional vendor setup. That is our problem, not the fab's.   For a scaler, the value is the artefact, not the agent. Claude never sat in QuEra's control loop. It developed the routine and handed over deterministic code. Agent in process development, script in production. That is a shape quality and audit can live with.   What it does not fix: an agent will not make a piezo stage settle faster. Alignment time per die is mechanics and physics.   Now look at who is building MHS support. Amazon Web Services (AWS), Danaher, Doosan Robotics, QIAGEN, Tecan, Universal Robots, Hugging FaceFace, Raspberry Pi Foundation. Life sciences and robotics company. Not one photonics test or alignment vendor. That is strange. Why not?    Our benches are already full of programmable instruments. SCPI and VISA have been standard for decades. An MHS driver for a tunable laser or an alignment stage is a smaller job than for most biology hardware, and the payoff is larger because our mix is worse. Xanadu, Project OPTIMISM LANDS AND ITS IMPACT ON THE GLOBAL QUANTUM SUPPLY CHAIN  In June, at the Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow, Xanadu's Chief Operating Officer told the room the company was setting up a 160,000 square foot facility in Toronto to bring heterogeneous integration in-house. On Thursday, August 27th, they got a loan, not a grant, with repayments set as a percentage of future revenue.   Rafal Janik was keynoting our photonic quantum computing session, the first time Xanadu had spoken at an Optica industry event. Asked from the floor in the clip below about supply chain concentration in thin film lithium niobate, he gave an answer that reads differently now:   "Global supply chains are absolutely an issue. The really good thing is that quantum has been identified as a strategic priority for pretty much every single government in the world, so everybody's trying to onshore a lot of these materials now."   Thursday was that sentence turning into a building.   The facility is called Inception. A former Campbell's soup plant in Etobicoke, anchoring a CAD 893 million project, 275 technical jobs. Cleanrooms for heterogeneous integration, round the clock wafer level test, a systems integration centre where modules are verified before they go into racks.   That is a packaging and assembly plant. The quantum computer is the customer.   Janik was explicit in Glasgow about why it has to exist. Xanadu runs three material stacks, silicon nitride, thin film lithium niobate and III-V, and building them separately is no longer sufficient. They have to be integrated. Heterogeneous integration is the bottleneck, and it is a packaging problem before it is a physics problem.   Now look at who supplies the tools. ASMPT Ltd, Bluefors, DISCO, EV Group, ficonTECTEC and 旺矽科技股份有限公司. Singapore, Finland, Japan, Austria, Germany, Taiwan. Three of the six are European. Canada is buying supply chain sovereignty, and a large part of that supply chain is European.   I do not say that as criticism. It is the honest shape of our industry. Nobody sets up a photonic packaging line alone, because the equipment base is thin and spread across firms that have each spent decades becoming very good at one step.   The caveat matters. A packaging plant does not solve fault tolerance. Heterogeneous integration at production yield is unproven at this scale, and Inception is announced rather than running. My read is that the durable asset is the line itself. If photonic fault tolerance takes longer than its advocates expect, Canada still owns a general-purpose photonic integration capability. Those are scarce, and they are useful to AI hardware, telecom and sensing, whatever happens to qubits.   For European photonics companies the lesson is not to envy the cheque. When a government funds quantum manufacturing, a large share of it lands on equipment vendors. Europe is strong there. That is a position to defend deliberately, not one to assume will hold.

David Huang's presentation (15 min) from the Optica OIM on Photonics in Ophthalmology & Vision Care August 25th is worth a wider audience. OCT did not win because it was the best physics. It won because someone could bill for it.   David Huang co-invented optical coherence tomography, and in this clip he tells the origin story himself. It began as close to a pure physics experiment, using light to measure time of flight and see below a surface, in Professor Fujimoto's lab at MIT while he was a PhD student.   Then the dates.   First publication, 1991. First patent, 1994. First FDA cleared system, from Humphrey Zeiss, 1996. First CPT code, meaning a clinician could finally charge for the scan, 1997.   Six years from paper to reimbursement.   Adoption followed the billing code. Once the scan could be paid for, the revenue funded better instruments, which widened the clinical case, which justified better reimbursement. OCT did not even have that code to itself. It shared 92135 with retinal thickness analysers, slit scan tomography and scanning laser polarimetry, and took the market on depth resolution.   Huang is unusually direct about the rest of it. Regulatory steps were easier then, the founders did everything right, and they were lucky. That is a more honest account of a technology transition than the field usually gives itself.   Three things from the clip worth your time.   OCT has its own Moore's law. Commercial scan speed doubles roughly every 2.7 years, and every jump in speed opens something new. Ultra-widefield imaging of almost the whole retina, which his group is applying to retinopathy of prematurity, capturing a neonate's full retina in about twenty seconds in infrared light that does not disturb the baby. OCT angiography down to the capillary, resolving four separate vascular plexuses inside a few hundred microns of tissue. Optoretinography, which detects photoreceptors lengthening by nanometres when they capture a photon, so you can map function and not only structure.  And on what limits the next step, his answer was speed, bounded by how much light you can safely put on a retina. AI acceleration is the open avenue. FDA clearance is what slows it down.   There is also a short exchange near the end I keep coming back to. Asked whether a portable system could catch sepsis in intensive care, Huang said it is technically very feasible, and that the real barriers are regulatory approval and the fact that intensive care doctors are not trained on OCT. In his words, it is alien technology to them. The instrument is ready before the clinic is.   We do not often get to hear how a technology actually crossed over, from the person who was there. Fifteen minutes from our two-hour Online Industry Meeting on photonics in ophthalmology and vision care.

PhotonPath went after scale-across, and did it on purpose. That is where the network stops pretending to be digital. Fibre-dependent loss, different gains from different amplifiers, spectral shapes that have to be held in place. Douglas put it plainly: they picked the part of the market where the analog problems are hardest, because that is the part they know how to handle.   Their answer is the nanoOCM, an optical channel monitor small enough to plug into a switch or a router. 500 millisecond scan time. Minus 35 dBm sensitivity. Douglas says it is the first pluggable OCM on the market, and that the pluggability, not the physics, is what customers react to first. No integration project. Parallel links between AI clusters need optical power that a silicon waveguide will not take at 23 to 25 dBm without nonlinearities showing up. AI GOES UNDERWATER. South Korea has moved an underwater AI data centre from concept to funded pilot. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has selected the area around ULSAN for a 51.1 billion won (35.4 million dollar) demonstration, with container-style server modules on the seabed at 20 metres and a commercial complex of up to 100,000 servers from 2031. Sealed modules that cannot be hand-serviced for five to seven years change the interconnect calculus, since optical links carry more bandwidth per pressure-rated feedthrough than copper.   Servers and other equipment will be housed in large units similar to shipping containers, which will be lowered to the seabed 20 meters below. These can be added like building blocks to expand the facility to as much as 100,000 servers.  Trials are slated to start as early as this year, with work on the commercial complex to begin in 2031. The containers will need to be able to resist pressures three times as high as standard atmospheric pressure. Safeguards against salt corrosion and condensation will also be crucial.  With these measures and temperature control technology, the aim is to keep the electronics working underwater for five to seven years. The project is being led by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST), which is under the oceans ministry. To find ways to build infrastructure efficiently on the seafloor, the government in January entered a technical tie-up with SK Telecom to draw on the company's expertise in data center operation. Lotte Engineering & Construction and steelmaker POSCO HOLDINGS are involved in the project as well. Robots will be developed for remote monitoring.   This is not a first, though. In 2020, 微軟 announced the results of an underwater data centre pilot project. In China, a commercial undersea data center has been built off the coast of Hainan province.  Onshore data centers large swaths of land to house servers as well as equipment for power generation and transmission. South Korea only has a quarter of Japan's landmass, and much of the terrain is mountainous. Usable land has been running short in recent years, and construction costs have soared, so developers are looking to the seafloor despite the technical challenges. South Korea is also developing technology for floating data centers. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co., Ltd. (HD KSOE) in July entered a partnership with France's 施耐德電氣 to develop power infrastructure and flotation technology.  Samsung Heavy Industries has received approval in principle in the U.S. and the U.K. for a floating data center design, and is teaming with a Greek shipowner on commercialization.

JAPAN JUST BET 150 BILLION YEN ON A MATERIAL MOST PEOPLE CANNOT NAME. For years, indium phosphide was the material our community had to explain to everyone else. Now it is the material everyone else is explaining to us.  Look at Japan.  On 16 June, JX Advanced Metals Corporation (company video below) committed up to 120 billion yen over four years to expand InP substrate capacity. The largest investment the company has ever made in this product line. New capacity in Hitachinaka alongside the existing Isohara Works, targeting 7 to 10 times current output. Counting the three earlier expansions since July 2025, the total is around 150 billion yen.  Two smaller details tell you more.  JX said it is opening discussions with customers about price revisions. Anyone who has bought substrates knows what that means. This has been a thin margin business for a long time, and the supplier has just noticed it is holding the constraint.  JX also now calls InP a future revenue pillar alongside its semiconductor sputtering targets. I have watched many companies say photonics is strategic. Committing 150 billion yen is a different kind of statement.  Why now is no mystery. Silicon guides light, modulates it, splits it. It does not generate it. Every 800G and 1.6T module, and every co-packaged optics architecture behind them, still needs an InP laser as its source. Lumentum's CEO Michael Hurlston said on 6 August that the InP supply and demand gap now exceeds DRAM and NAND. Orders that used to arrive in the hundreds from telecom customers now arrive in the hundreds of millions of devices.  What I find most interesting is that three regions are answering the same question in three different ways.  The United States is answering with capital. NVIDIA put 2 billion dollars each into Coherent Corp. and Lumentum in March, with long-term supply agreements attached. Coherent broke ground in Texas in June on a 6-inch InP fab expansion, backed by a proposed 50 million dollar US CHIPS Act grant.  China is answering with integration. Yunnan Chihong Zinc&Germanium Co., Ltd. scaling 6 inch substrates, San'An Optoelectronics Co., Ltd. running substrate to chip in a single house. Remember, China also refines roughly 70 percent of the world's indium and has tightened export controls since 2025.  Japan is answering with depth. JX is not moving downstream into lasers or modules. It is making itself the layer nobody can design around.  None of this rescues 2027. Indium comes out of zinc refining as a by-product, so the feedstock does not respond to demand signals. Large diameter InP crystal growth takes years of patient yield work. Analysts expect the imbalance to run past 2027, and JX's new capacity arrives late in the decade.  So what do we conclude? The bottleneck in AI infrastructure right now is not a transistor problem. It is a crystal growth problem. Photonics is no longer the interesting adjacent field. It is the critical path. LASERS ARE THE QUIET HEART OF THE Einstein Telescope Last week I sat down with Stefan Hild, Project Director of ET Pathfinder, at the test facility in  #Maastricht. What I saw changed how I think about the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and about the role industry plays in getting one built.  ET Pathfinder exists to prove out the technology for the Einstein Telescope, the successor to LIGO and Virgo. The ambition: measure the distance between two test masses 10 meters apart to a precision of 10⁻¹⁸ meters. Stefan's comparison stuck with me. It is the equivalent of dropping a single drop of water into the Mediterranean and detecting the rise in sea level. Getting there takes two things working in tandem. The test masses have to be kept extremely still, through vacuum systems and seismic isolation. Then a laser has to detect whether they move at all, and that is where the real difficulty sits. The laser needs a stable reference: here, a 10-meter cavity with silicon mirrors cooled to cryogenic temperatures to cut thermal noise. Even the cooling has to be engineered around the laser. Sorption coolers with no moving parts are used instead of mechanical compressors, so the act of cooling doesn't introduce the vibration you're trying to eliminate. Beyond that, quantum effects start to matter. Squeezed light and quantum non-demolition techniques are being tested to work around the limits set by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle itself.  None of this happens without industry. Stefan was direct about it: six industry consortia in the Netherlands, backed by around 12 million euros in funding, are already developing the vibration-free cryocoolers this facility needs. The same technology is finding its way into electron microscopy, superconducting motors for lithography, quantum computing cooling and infrared imaging. And as the project scales toward a multi-billion euro facility meant to run for 50 years, industry brings something physicists don't have on their own: systems engineering, quality assurance and risk management at that level.  ET Pathfinder has already drawn 25 research institutions from 8 countries. A newly secured 29 million euro expansion will add larger clean rooms and taller test towers, preparing the ground for a facility Stefan expects will eventually involve around 2,000 researchers across Europe.  The Einstein Telescope will tell us about the universe. Getting there is being built, quite literally, on light.

BREAKING: NVIDIA JUST BACKED A SPANISH OPTICAL SWITCH COMPANY. THE INTERESTING PART IS WHICH KIND OF SWITCH. iPRONICS , a Valencia spin-off from Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), has raised $125 million in a Series B co-led by Maverick Silicon and Light Street Capital, with NVIDIA in the round. Total funding is now $177 million. Nineteen months ago its Series A was 20 million euros.   The headline number is not the story. Three details matter more.   First, the technology. Optical circuit switching is not new. Google has run MEMS-based optical switches as the backbone of its data centre networks for nearly a decade and says it deployed tens of thousands of them. Lumentum's R300 is MEMS too. Coherent Corp. uses liquid crystal. iPronics is doing it in silicon photonics: no mirrors, no moving parts, the light is steered inside the chip. MEMS switches reconfigure in milliseconds today. The silicon photonics bet is that no moving parts wins on speed and unit cost once volumes matter.   Second, the investor. In March NVIDIA put $2 billion each into Lumentum and Coherent and joined the $500 million round at Ayar Labs. It is now in a much smaller company that competes with two of those three on switching. My read is that NVIDIA is not picking a winner. It is buying optionality on every layer where copper runs out.   Third, the target. The release talks about scale-up networking, the fabric inside and across racks that ties GPUs into one machine. That is the segment where Lumentum and Marvell demonstrated OCS in March. It is also the hardest place to put a switch, because loss budgets and port counts are unforgiving. The physics here is simple: every extra decibel of insertion loss costs you reach or laser power, and a switch with fewer ports means more layers of switching.   Now the caveat. The release names no customer, no port count, no insertion loss and no shipment volume. "Tier-one partners" is doing a lot of work in that text. Lumentum has told investors it expects OCS revenue meaningfully above $100 million in a single quarter. iPronics still has to prove it can build and deliver at scale, though its Santa Clara office has been operational since last December. Cignal AI puts the OCS market at $2.5 billion or more by 2029. That is a real market. It is not yet a decided one.   What this means for our community is the bigger point. For a decade, optical circuit switching was one hyperscaler's private tool. Since 2024 it has become a merchant market with MEMS, liquid crystal and silicon photonics all funded to compete, and a European university spin-off now sits at the table with $177 million behind it. That is what a working photonics ecosystem looks like: several physical approaches, real money on each, and the customer deciding.

DESIGN FOR THE ROTOR BLADE, NOT FOR THE CHIP: PHOTONFIRST GRAND TOUR PART ONE Most conversations about photonic packaging start with the chip. For defence, that is already the wrong starting point. We went to PhotonFirst in Alkmaar, The Netherlands, because at Optica we want to understand how the photonics supply chain actually looks for defence applications. European governments are raising the share of GDP they spend on defence. Our industry keeps saying photonics is strategic. I wanted to see what that means on a factory floor.   Jan-Jurien de Rijck walked me through the cleanroom, and gave me the comparison that stayed with me. A data centre against an Apache helicopter. Put a system on a rotor blade and shock, vibration and electromagnetic compatibility stop being tests you run at the end. They set the design from the first day.   The standards do the talking. DO-160 in the civil domain. MIL-STD-461 for EMC and MIL-STD-810 for shock, vibration and moisture ingress in the military domain. Those requirements flow down from system level to package level, which is the reason the package cannot be designed after the chip is finished.   One process makes it concrete. The fibre-to-chip connection has long been the weak point in these systems. PhotonFirst uses lensed fibre laser welding rather than adhesive, because glue struggles under thermal load. Fibre array welding is still in development.   And there is a product to point at rather than a capability claim. A digital sun sensor for satellite navigation, qualified to DO-160, built in the hundreds on a dedicated production line.   For twenty years we have told people to think about the package before the chip. What I heard in Alkmaar goes one step further back. Think about the environment first, then the system, then the package, then the chip.   My read is that this is the part of the supply chain Europe consistently underestimates. We argue about foundries and about chips. The step that decides whether a photonic system survives a rotor blade is packaging and qualification, and the number of European companies that can take that all the way to a qualified system is small. THIS CONFERENCE WORKS BECAUSE PEOPLE SAY WHAT THEY NEED Most industry events are showcases. Ours is built the other way round. Every speaker at the recent Optica Quantum Industry Summit gets the same two questions: what can you do for others, and what can others do for you. The enabling technologies session opened with the chair telling the room that end users and integrators should say what they actually need, not what they already sell.  Tim Day, Chairman and Chief Executive of Monarch Quantum, took fifteen minutes and used almost none of it on physics.  Monarch is six months old. The playbook is not. Day has spent three decades moving photonics out of the laboratory and into production. He co-founded New Focus, which built photonics subsystems for telecom hardware, took it public and merged it with a British multinational. He then did the same in aerospace and defence, a business he says is close to shipping a billion dollars of photonic subsystems and turns over 150 to 200 million a year. Monarch was spun out of that work to serve quantum. Around 120 engineers and scientists, in San Diego.  His opening claim is the one worth arguing about. In the quantum systems he works on, photonics is 40 to 65 per cent of the bill of materials.  Then he did the arithmetic. A 10,000-qubit machine can involve more than 100,000 optical components. Give every component a 10,000-hour lifetime, put them in series, and the system lasts six minutes! That is the case against carrying laboratory instruments into products. Not that they perform badly. They perform beautifully. They cannot be manufactured and they cannot stay up.  Monarch’s answer is co-packaged optics for quantum, re-engineered from the bond joint up and assembled robotically. He was careful about PICs. They will matter, but they do not yet cover UV to near infrared at the losses quantum needs, so micro-optic packaging does the work today.  The useful part was what he found underneath everyone’s different architecture. About a dozen recurring functions. Narrow linewidth lasers in several colours, electro-optic and acousto-optic modulation, amplitude control, fibre launch, amplify and split, replicating one frequency across six to twelve channels. Standardise those and you have a platform, built in automated work cells, at red, green, blue and near infrared instead of telecom wavelengths. He is deliberately agnostic. Atom, ion or photon based, he does not claim to know which wins, only that quantum does.  He is building a factory with more than 25 production work cells. Monarch holds more than 60 million dollars in customer contracts and raised 55 million this year. His answer to the Optica question was a request, not a pitch. Tell him what subsystems you need and he will tell you whether it is already on the platform.  That is the conversation our industry is short of.

WHY IonQ TOOK THE OPTICS OUT OF ITS MOST IMPORTANT OPERATION Mihir Bhaskar opened his keynote at the recent Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow with a line that should stop a photonics audience. IonQ has moved the two-qubit gate, the hardest operation in a trapped ion computer, off the lasers and onto an RF line in the chip. His reasoning was blunt.   Optics are harder to engineer, scale and integrate than electronics.  Nine things worth taking from his excellent talk- worth watching in full on Youtube. https://lnkd.in/eehmD3ni  IonQ has changed shape. Eighteen months ago it was a quantum computing company. It is now four lines: computing, networking, security and sensing. watch their 2026 Investor event on September 8th. https://lnkd.in/e86pVFbh The most critical operation is electronic now. Control is integrated into the trap chip, built on more than a decade of work in Oxford. He quotes about 99.99 per cent two qubit gate fidelity, and a trap that scales as a 2D grid using semiconductor fabrication.  Photonics moved rather than left. Cooling and readout stay optical and are being integrated into zones on the trap. Getting to 10,000 qubits is largely a photonic integration problem.  The interconnect problem is a loss problem with a number on it. About 20 dB to get a photon from an ion into single mode fibre, the same as 100 km of SMF-28. Paid at both ends, that is one success in 10,000 attempts.  Quantum memory is the fix, and the processor does not change. A memory between two processors lets the link run asynchronously. His figures: around 99 per cent storage fidelity, about 3 dB heralding loss, over 100 MHz bandwidth.  Diamond is becoming manufacturable. Thin film diamond, with Element Six in the UK. His comparison: diamond today looks like lithium niobate ten years ago.  A packaging spec you can hold a supplier to. Below 0.2 dB waveguide to fibre at visible wavelengths, in diamond, silicon nitride, silicon, lithium niobate and III-Vs. Not yet space qualified.  The economics work in the data centre first. Interconnect is 20 to 40 per cent of the cost of an NVIDIA cluster, so a quantum interconnect can be expensive and still be viable. A dated roadmap. 2026, the network runs faster than the processor. 2027, multiple channels and compatibility with other platforms. 2028, logical qubits moving between processors.
